articles.title: London in drought: 'We need to change how we think about water'
articles.summary: Experts say a changing climate and increasing demand for water will mean people need to make changes.
articles.body:
Hyde Park looks more like the Serengeti and the green belt has turned yellow. But with London now seeing the occasional shower, does that mean we are no longer in drought? And if not, the big question is how long will the drought last?

The capital is particularly susceptible to drought as there is a very large population, in an area that is actually very dry. Experts call it "water stressed."

The myth is London is a rainy city, yet the capital gets less rain than many other cities in Europe.

According to the Met Office the Thames Valley, London and the north Kent coast normally receive less than 650mm (26in) of rain every year. By comparison, Rome gets up to 900mm (35in).

SES Water covers parts of Surrey, Kent and south London and at the moment it is one of the few water companies that doesn't have a hosepipe ban.

Daniel Kennedy, the firm's water services director, says it is impossible to predict when the drought will end.

"We do model our position with where we think things might go, but a lot of it is determined by the hot weather and the prolonged dry period that we've had."

He says water companies "are looking forward to when the rain does come because it does ease the position somewhat. But until it happens, it's really difficult to say how long it'll go on for.

"We would want a sustained period of rain... so we can replenish our groundwater stocks and our reservoirs, to enable us to have water in supply in our reserves for next year."

Liz Stephens is a professor in climate risks and resilience at the University of Reading.

She thinks it could take months to get back to normal, noting that previous hosepipe bans in parts of the South East were only lifted "towards the end of January, early February", while "the Thames Water hosepipe ban lifted towards the end of November".

"It really does depend on the amount of rainfall that we get. If we see a dry autumn and winter, and we don't see that recharge of groundwater, the rise in reservoir levels, potentially we could be looking at similar restrictions next summer as well," she says.

There is even a possibility this drought might not come to an end this year, according to Stephens.

"If we don't get the amount of rain that's needed, then there will be a lot of concern about the water supply going into next spring and summer as well. We probably would then expect further restrictions.

"The 1976 drought came after a period of low winter rainfall as well. And in that situation that summer there were the standpipes on the streets for water supply," she says.

Most of the capital's water comes from chalk aquifers under the ground. These take much longer to recharge than reservoirs.

Stephens also points out that while water companies may have been preparing for a prolonged drought, they are now facing other issues as well.

"They might not have been able to anticipate the type of demands that we're now seeing in the South East, not just from the increase in population, but also the very recent increase in data centres and the demand that they're putting on water as well."

Reservoir levels are currently at about 70%, which is lower than usual at this time of year.

Martin Padley, water director at Thames Water, which does have a hosepipe ban , says the company is grateful to everyone for reducing their water use, but given the current situation "we're asking customers to keep going and continue using only what they need.

"Small changes, such as taking shorter showers, turning off taps and avoiding non-essential water use outdoors, all help reduce pressure on our network while our teams continue working around the clock to find and fix leaks."

More than two-thirds of England now in drought

Keeping London's canal boats afloat during drought

Looking down on London's straw-coloured parks

Long-term water scarcity is becoming more of an issue in London and the South East.

No major reservoirs have been completed in England since 1992. But a growing population and developments like new data centres are putting intense pressure on our water supplies.

Also, climate change is bringing hotter, drier summers that increase the risk of drought.

The government's solution is to build nine new reservoirs by 2050, potentially providing 670 million litres of extra water daily.

But some experts say we're thinking about water all wrong.

Hannah Cloke, professor of hydrology at the School of Archaeology, Geography and Environmental Science at the University of Reading, believes "we need a complete overhaul of the way we use water".

"We need to plug leaks, cut down on waste and use water more than once in our homes and buildings before sloshing it down the drain. We need to catch more water wherever it falls – not just in the river basins that are linked to big reservoirs," she says.

"An unprecedented climate calls for unprecedented solutions," adds Cloke.

"These could include the widespread roll out of sustainable drainage solutions that mimic nature and capture rainwater where it falls, on roofs or ditches filled with plants, rather than letting it rush straight down the drains into the rivers."

And one of the big unknowns long term is data centres.

Stephens says they're making an enormous difference.

"Thames Water had been trying to predict demand over the next 10 years... They've estimated that about 30% of that increased demand is coming from the growth of data centres.

"And I think they've already admitted that they're underestimating the demand that's happened so far from those data centres. It's an incredible amount of water that these centres use."

A huge new reservoir is planned to be built in Oxfordshire, called the White Horse Reservoir , to improve water supply.

However, Stephens says that while it will cover "a very large area of land, actually, by the time it's built, it might already be out of date.

"The extra volume that it's going to supply is roughly equivalent to that sort of upper estimate of the demand from data centres. So these really are crazy amounts of water that these data centres can use."

Kennedy, from SES Water, says we will have to use water wisely throughout the year, especially with a changing climate.

This includes the likes of having shorter showers, turning the tap off when cleaning your teeth and making sure washing machines and dishwashers are only run when they are fully loaded, he says.

"If we can use water wisely all year round, it will obviously help us with our stocks in the times of the year when we really need it.

"The world is changing and we've had five heatwaves already this summer. So people are starting to understand that water is a precious commodity," he says.

At the moment, about 20% of water is lost through leaks. Thames Water says it is investing a record amount £21bn in fixing them. Critics say that is too little, too late.

Thames Water has also estimated that it could face a daily shortfall of over one billion litres of water by 2050. The funding needed for improvements and new water systems will be significant.

Its proposals include the new reservoir in Oxfordshire and a water recycling project in west London at Teddington. Both have faced opposition.

To match the demand, Thames Water is also striving to reduce daily water use to 110 litres per person by 2050, with current water use in the area at about 140 litres per person.

In other words, all of us will have to use less water.

In the face of a hotter climate, the mayor of London has created a heat plan, called Heat Ready London , which also highlights behaviour change as crucial.

It says: "Alongside infrastructure upgrades, changes in behaviours and system operation are essential to reduce pressure on water supplies.

"To enhance long-term water security, investment should be scaled up through a portfolio-based and integrated water management approach, recognising that no single intervention can address future challenges in isolation.

"A balanced portfolio of measures – including smart meters, active leakage reduction, water-efficiency initiatives, water recycling and reuse, rainwater harvesting, and targeted new supply schemes – should be implemented in a co-ordinated manner to deliver greater resilience and adaptability across the entire water system."

Experts say the whole water system needs a rethink to make it fit for the future.

Certainly, with a warming climate this won't be the last hosepipe ban in London and the South East.

articles.title: Songs created by AI banned from Australia's music charts
articles.summary: The move comes weeks after a DJ admitted using AI to remix a Madonna song that topped the Australian charts.
articles.body:
Songs that are largely or wholly created by AI have been banned from Australia's music charts.

From this week, all releases must be "substantially human made" to be eligible.

The Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) said the new code would help "promote the human nature of artistry".

It follows a controversy around a cover of Madonna's Like A Prayer by Australian DJ Josh Fawaz which recently topped the ARIA dance singles chart and peaked at number 2 on the country's overall chart.

The song has become a staple of commercial radio station playlists and been streamed more than 48 million times on Spotify alone.

Fawaz later added generative AI credits to the song after a backlash.

ARIA said that Australian artists were competing for attention "in the most crowded market in history" and that it was "not interested in promoting or celebrating the success of AI-generated music that does not contain human artistry".

Under the new rules, AI assistance can still be used, but humans must have written the song, and have performed the lead vocal and primary instruments.

AI can also still be used for mastering songs and, for example, using drum machines and auto tune.

Earlier this year a song was banned from Sweden's music charts because it was created by AI.

And in July, the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) said AI guidelines would be rolled out in Latin America, the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia for use in their official charts.

The updated code, based on the IFPI directive, also excludes music that raises "stream or chart manipulation concerns".

ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said: "These changes reflect our intent to remain dynamic and promote the human nature of artistry in what is, to say the least, a rapidly developing space."

"Artists already use AI tools in their work, the charts can and should evolve to keep room for that, but music generated wholesale by services built on artists' recordings is a different matter."

She added: "A chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent."

Artists will be required to declare AI use when they submit a song for chart consideration.

ARIA said that if it later emerged music was largely AI-generated it could retrospectively adjust chart positions, and if the piece topped the charts, it may request that awards given for reaching Number One were returned.

Artists and their representatives will be able to challenge their exclusion.

Among the artists supporting the move are Australian electronic act Peking Duk.

Last month, they shared an AI-assisted version of their 2014 hit High on Instagram, captioned: "When you re-record your own song with AI so Australian radio will play it."

Band member Adam Hyde told Channel Nine's Today show that AI-generated music was "removing the human experience from life".

In July this year, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese promised "the strongest possible protection" from AI for Australian creatives.

Albanese pledged that writers and musicians would be able to choose if and how their work was used in the training of AI, saying it would be "theft" if creatives lost that control and were not paid for its use.

articles.title: Goat sanctuary purchases 16.9 acres of more land in Kent
articles.summary: The land purchased by Buttercups Sanctuary for Goats will enable it to house up to 160 goats.
articles.body:
A goat sanctuary in Kent has purchased an additional 16.9 acres of land, which it said would enable it to house up to 160 goats.

Buttercups Sanctuary for Goats in Boughton Monchelsea said that the new plot of land was close to where it was currently situated and would provide "long-lasting results for both our adorable residents and the wider, beautiful countryside".

Matt Huggins said that it was the "most significant step since the charity's foundation".

"It's been something we've all been dreaming of for a long, long time, and we're all very excited to get going," Huggins added.

According to the sanctuary, the purchased plot of land had historically been used for agriculture and will enable it to rescue more goats and double its on-site capacity.

It said a lot of work would need to be carried out on the land despite being a "blank canvas", but new goats are expected to begin living there by spring 2027.

Huggins added that its long-term vision included solar panels, wind turbines and habitat networks for the wildlife, which he expected would take years to be fully completed.

"There's a long road ahead, and we are going to need the help of our supporters to make it a final reality, but we've taken the first major step," he said.

articles.title: Whisky barrel bought for £130 goes on sale at £270,000
articles.summary: Pensioner Angus Kerr bought the cask of Glenrothes single malt in 1971 for £130 as an investment.
articles.body:
A whisky barrel purchased for £130 is to go on sale for £270,000.

Surrey pensioner Angus Kerr said he had bought the Glenrothes single malt in 1971 as an investment, hoping it would help pay for his children's school fees.

He said it was now worth an "unbelievable" sum, as the barrel was the oldest of its kind known to be in existence.

"I don't drink scotch," Kerr said. "If I did, I would be looking around for something that was £18, no more. That's my sort of level."

Kerr, a former commodities trader, said he had made the purchase after hearing about a company selling barrels of new-fill whisky.

"I thought at least I can go for a swim in it if it all goes belly up," he told BBC Radio Surrey .

Kerr said he had hoped to sell the barrel five years later for a profit, but the company went bust and he lost contact with them.

"I just threw my hands in the air and thought, 'OK, that was silly'," he added.

However, a few years later, the 81-year-old was contacted out of the blue by a Glaswegian company, which said he owed them money for storing the barrel.

After getting waylaid by "business, kids and life in general", Kerr said he had only recently contacted broker Mark Littler to try to sell the barrel, which contains enough for approximately 287 bottles.

Kerr said the tasting experts had declared the 57-year-old whisky "absolutely fantastic".

"It could have lost its alcohol content or ended up being very oaky and horrible, so it's very fortunate," he added.

"What we need to find is Elon Musk, [Jeff] Bezos or someone for who £270,000 is just spare change to them."

On how he would spend the proceeds, Kerr said he would not have any "difficulty finding a home for the money" with his children and eight grandchildren.

"But it goes pretty quickly these days," he added.

articles.title: Somerset cider makers left with very few apples after heatwaves
articles.summary: Some orchards are harvesting just a 10th of their usual crop, and facing an uncertain future.
articles.body:
Somerset's famous cider orchards have been "decimated" by the long summer drought, producers say. Many trees have produced no fruit at all, and others have dropped their fruit early, rotting before they ripened.

"It's gut-wrenching," says Kimberly Jones of Honey's Cider near Bath, whose orchard has produced only a 10th of its normal amount of apples.

Neil MacDonald, who manages more than 1,000 acres of Somerset orchards, says he has watched half his apples fall before they have ripened, because the trees are stressed by the drought.

"Nothing sells cider like sunshine," he says, "and we've emptied our tanks.

"The sadness is we haven't got enough fruit to refill the tanks again."

Walking through Kimberly Jones' orchard just outside Bath, it's hard to see any apples at all. The trees should be groaning with fruit, she tells me, but "we might get 10% of our normal crop here, and that's generous".

The orchard is 25 years old, and this is by far the driest year they have had. Because 2025 was also dry, the trees became stressed, she explained, and this year most have just not made fruit at all, to save their energy.

Unlike the big commercial brands, Honey's Cider is only made from fresh juice. Jones refuses to buy apple concentrate or industrial products.

"So we can only make cider from the juice we make each year, which means we will be down this year," she adds.

Ironically, the long hot summer has been "brilliant" for actually selling cider.

"Everyone likes a cold cider on a hot day, but we are struggling now to grow fruit for next year," Jones says.

On one of Somerset's most famous cider farms, I hear the same story. Gordon Rich started pressing apples on a farm near Highbridge in 1954. Today his grandson George Scott makes nearly a million litres of cider a year.

"We would normally harvest 20-30 tonnes of apples here," he tells me, walking through one orchard.

"There's so little fruit in here I won't even put the harvester in - the sheep can have any that drop."

Neighbouring farms that Scott buys from are also short of fruit. One grower who normally produces 200 tonnes is "down to about 30", he adds.

Will his tanks run dry then, I wondered?

"No, we've got plenty of cider in the tanks for now," he smiles. Cider makers can keep stock from year to year, but Scott says he worries about the future of his trees.

Two years of drought have already stressed them, and climate scientists are warning farmers to expect more hot dry summers .

"I do worry that next year will show a lot more signs of the drought and the trees will be stressed again. If we get another dry year, I don't know what we're going to do," he adds.

Not every orchard is bare, of course. Neil MacDonald manages more than 1,000 acres of cider orchards across Somerset. At his Orchard Park Farm, near Shepton Mallet, I see plenty of apples - both on the trees and on the ground.

With a roar, the apple harvester starts up. It powers down the rows, sweeping up the apples under the trees, up and away into the trailer.

This is at least three weeks' early for harvest, but they are not picking up the fruit to make cider.

"All these apples will go on the compost heap," MacDonald tells me, ruefully.

He cuts one open to show me the inside, mottled brown and floury.

"It's unripe, but it's already rotted before we've even started," he explains.

"The trees are stressed without any water, so they've just dumped the fruit on the ground to save themselves."

The harvester sweeps along, filling a large trailer with cider apples that Neil and his team have spent all year trying to grow, only to throw away.

"We've probably lost about half the crop this way," he says.

"This should be a 20-tonne orchard. If I get 10 tonnes from it I'll be grateful."

Somerset's cider apple growers know this is not a freak year.

"What we used to think of as extreme weather, we increasingly consider as normal." says Mike Kendon, a climate scientist at the Met Office .

But what can an apple grower do about it?

Neil MacDonald is now watering newly planted trees.

"Five years ago you would just dig a good hole and leave nature to get on with it," he smiles.

"Now you can't get away with that, you have to irrigate young trees or they die."

But irrigation for hundreds of acres of cider orchards is "just not viable", he said. Farmers who grow eating apples for supermarkets command higher prices for their fruit, so traditionally they have invested in irrigation systems.

Cider growers are now having to rethink their calculations.

Most fundamentally of all, climate change may actually change the taste of West Country cider.

One of the main varieties that gives Somerset cider its bittersweet taste is Dabinett. Several growers have found these trees producing very few apples this year, not because of the drought, but the mild winter.

"Dabinett needs a cold snap," MacDonald explains. "We just didn't get the cold winter days this year or last, so it's not producing."

He is now grafting other varieties onto his Dabinett trees, plants that fare better in hot dry weather.

As our climate changes, the very taste of Somerset cider may change too.

articles.title: The Gurkha families in Reading fighting for their pensions
articles.summary: Gurkhas who retired before 1997 receive far less than their British Army counterparts.
articles.body:
Now aged 87, Indumati Thapa's life revolves around a group of similarly widowed women. Her husband, a former Gurkha who fought alongside the British in south east Asia, died in 2020.

He left her a pension, but Gurkhas who retired before 1997 receive far less than their British Army counterparts.

Theirs are based on Nepalese living costs, not those of towns like Reading, where thousands of Gurkhas retired to.

Indumati says her pension is so small she has to rely on the generosity of friends, and roughly £100 a week in benefits, to cover her rent, bills and food costs.

The government says it "holds the distinguished service of the Gurkhas in the highest regard and remains firmly committed to supporting the welfare of Gurkha veterans and their families".

Many Gurkhas disagree and want their pensions increased.

Indumati lives in a small two-bedroom flat with her friend Devisara Rana in central Reading.

Squeezing into her small bedroom I ask her how she feels about her life.

Her friend and local Labour councillor Pratikshya Gurung translates for her.

"She thinks they've been let down a bit and says she would be grateful if the pension was bigger than it is as that would make her living conditions and financial situation better," Pratikshya says.

For those whose husbands fought for the British in the jungles of places like Malaya and Borneo in the1950s and 60s time is now running out.

The Labour MP for Reading Central Matt Rodda says he is well aware of that fact, and he and other MPs have been pressing both the previous Conservative government and the current Labour one to improve older Gurkha's pension rights.

He says he is also trying to make sure they and their families get all the help they need.

Unable to read or write, many of them rely on younger relations to navigate the modern world, one very different from the land they grew up in.

The Labour MP says: "It's so important we show our support for these elderly people. They served this country with distinction over decades and decades."

The Ministry of Defence says: "The government holds the distinguished service of the Gurkhas in the highest regard and remains firmly committed to supporting the welfare of Gurkha veterans and their families.

"We will continue to work with partners in both Nepal and the UK to ensure Gurkha veterans and their families receive the support and recognition they deserve."

With Pratikshya again translating, I speak to Indumati's close friend Devisara Rana, whose husband and son are no longer with us.

She says she is at peace with the fact all her worldly possessions fit in a bedroom that is no more than 12ft long, by eight feet wide.

Pratikshya tells me all Devisara wants now is to go back to Nepal, but fears she will be unable to afford the trip.

"She doesn't know how long she has got to live but that however many days she does have left she wants to spend those days with her family," she says.

"She just wants to be able to go home one last time."

articles.title: Avian botulism outbreak 'new norm' as hundreds die at Rye Harbour
articles.summary: Hundreds of birds have died at Rye Harbour Nature Reserve from avian botulism, say conservationists.
articles.body:
A conservation group has warned that avian botulism outbreaks will become more common due to climate change after more than a hundred birds died in East Sussex.

The birds died after a suspected outbreak of the disease at Rye Harbour Nature Reserve, according to Sussex Wildlife Trust.

The charity's head of nature reserves, Jamie Parsons, said that as heatwaves and droughts become more common, "more outbreaks are going to come along with them".

"This is something we have to get used to and become resilient to in a changing climate," he told the BBC.

The UK has experienced a record-breaking summer of extreme heat and prolonged dry weather.

A resulting fall in river levels has had a significant impact on wetland ecosystems in the region.

Experts are warning that climate change means the UK is experiencing more frequent intense winter storms followed by heatwaves and droughts in summers.

The consensus among scientists is that human activities are causing climate change .

Avian botulism is a neurological disease caused by a toxin. The bacterium that produces the toxin thrives in warm, shallow, oxygen-lacking water.

The wildlife trust attributed the East Sussex outbreak to recent hot and dry conditions causing "water levels to fall significantly, creating conditions in which the toxin can develop".

Parsons said this had become "the new norm for us as conservationists and land managers".

"It's devastating really," he said. "It's heartbreaking and frustrating.

"The team works so hard to make sure that the reserve is as good as it can be for the species that live here and they put in all that work.

"Then something out of our control happens and causes this disease outbreak," Parsons said.

There have been other suspected outbreaks of avian botulism in the UK, including in Bristol .

Visitors to Rye Harbour are being urged to avoid contact with water and not touch sick, injured or dead animals.

Castle Water, covering about half of the nature reserve, has been closed to the public due to the outbreak.

Dr Oluwole Oni, lecturer in intensive animal health at the University of Surrey, said the public should keep pets on leads as animals "wouldn't become infected" if kept away from the contaminated areas.

"If you see any of these birds, you just want to quickly report it to the right authority," Oni said.

articles.title: Medieval Guernsey reading habits revealed in hidden manuscripts
articles.summary: Archivists discover 17 manuscript fragments from medieval times were repurposed as book covers.
articles.body:
Seventeen fragments of medieval manuscripts that had been "hidden in plain sight" for centuries have been uncovered in Guernsey.

Offering insight into the island's early literary culture, the fragments suggest late medieval Guernsey was home to keen readers, and reading in French rather than English was preferred.

Also regarded as "striking early examples of recycling", historians found the fragments were repurposed as covers for notebooks and bindings for administrative records, meaning they were unknowingly preserved.

Prof Tamara Atkin, a book historian from the University of Oxford, said the discovery "transforms what we can now say about Guernsey's medieval manuscript culture".

Until now there had been virtually no evidence for libraries, collections of books or literary culture in the island during the medieval period, said the States of Guernsey.

Atkin said the discovery showed "books of several kinds - scholastic, liturgical, and literary - were available on the island" at the time.

The fragments - found in the Island Archives and His Majesty's Greffier's strongroom - were identified by the archive team working alongside Atkin and manuscript expert Dr David Rundle, from the University of Kent.

It began when archival assistant Callum Tostevin-Hall was asked to track down a 16th Century copy of Edward III's 1331 Extente of Guernsey, which detailed the Crown's rights in the island.

During his research, he noticed the shelfmark contained a reference to a vellum cover with Latin text that had been removed from the notebook in a previous round of conservation.

"I checked this cover and was astonished to find that it was clearly a reused bifolium from a medieval manuscript," he said.

"Taken together the fragments give an unprecedented glimpse into Guernsey's medieval past, which is not only very exciting for the Island Archives as an institution, but also for me personally as a medievalist."

The team said many of the fragments were in Latin but six of them were in French, with most being popular works that survive in several copies across England and France.

One comes from a dramatic poem called L'Estoire de Griseldis, a secular play thought to have been written by Philippe de Mézières around 1395.

Versions of the Griselda story were popular across late medieval Europe but the version found in the Guernsey fragment was said by the team to be "exceptionally rare".

Island archivist Vikki Hart said the reuse of the fragments as book covers showed resourcefulness "is nothing new in Guernsey".

"What was once a practical act of reusing old parchment has, centuries later, preserved pieces of the island's history that would otherwise have been lost," she said.

articles.title: Jersey earnings rise by 1.2% after inflation
articles.summary: Statistics Jersey says the increase is "slightly lower" than the long-term annual average.
articles.body:
Average earnings in Jersey did not keep up with the rate of inflation for the year to June, according to new figures.

Statistics Jersey said in June 2026 earnings per full-time equivalent employee was 4.1% higher than in June 2025.

However, once adjusted for inflation - currently at 2.8% for the island , external - Statistics Jersey said earnings rose by 1.2%, representing a real-terms pay cut.

The Index of Average Earnings June 2026 report , external said the overall increase was lower than the preceding five-year annual average of 5.6% per year and "slightly lower" than the long-term annual average of 4.2% per year for 1991 to 2025.

It also highlighted average earnings in real terms increased by 0.9% in the private sector and 2.9% in the public sector over 12 years.

However, it said, over 25 years, average earnings in real terms in the public sector decreased by 3% while they increased by 1.2% in the private sector.

Statistics Jersey said the report was determined from earnings data collected from a large representative survey of employers and all Government of Jersey departments.

It said this was the fourth year in which the survey was compulsory for employers to complete.

Matthew Gill, a statistician for Statistics Jersey, said, when looking back at figures going back to 2001, there had not been much a change in real-term earnings.

He said: "It's not necessarily that people are earning less.

"With inflation going up, it is generally something that people will notice more.

"A lot of the inflation recently has been things like petrol, which people notice when topping up their cars and has an effect on deliveries for food and that type of thing."

Heidi Gibaut, executive director at Law At Work, said a lot of the firm's clients had taken on secondary roles to boost their income.

She said: "When I was younger, I did two roles; but it's not a sustainable way of living.

"It's not how you will get the best out of the colleagues that you currently work with."

Gibaut said she felt it was down to employers to make sure the services and products they offered were being done at the right price to stop inflation from getting worse and "ensure colleagues are paid well".

"But it is a really, really hard balance," she added.

articles.title: Tech Town project equips Barnsley jobseekers with AI skills
articles.summary: New courses in Barnsley will offer training as well as paid work placements.
articles.body:
Barnsley residents will be offered support in using artificial intelligence (AI) to train for future careers under two new government schemes.

AI Career Launchpad will offer flexible training and paid work placements with employers, while Getting Job Ready with AI will support jobseekers, the Cabinet Office said.

The training comes six months after Barnsley was dubbed the UK's first "Tech Town", with firms including Microsoft, Cisco and Adobe pledging to support local people seeking "jobs of the future".

AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said: "AI is going to transform the world of work and our job is to make sure working people benefit from that change."

He added: "That starts with helping people understand how AI can be useful day-to-day - whether that means finding a job, learning new skills or building a career in a growing industry.

"Barnsley is showing what this can look like in practice.

"As our first Tech Town, it is helping us find ways that can create opportunities for local people and support communities across the country."

The AI Career Launchpad, a partnership with Barnsley College worth more than £400,000, will offer residents of all ages a faster, more flexible route into AI jobs.

Learners will get six months of training linked to a Level 4 apprenticeship, plus paid placements to gain experience while they learn.

Barnsley College Principal and CEO David Akeroyd said the scheme opened up careers that had, until now, been "concentrated elsewhere in the country".

Local businesses that sign up will benefit by getting early access to people training in AI, with government-funded placements helping them bring fresh skills into their teams.

Once the programme has been completed, its curriculum will then be freely available for other colleges and training providers elsewhere to use across the country.

From September, jobseekers in Barnsley will also get hands-on support through the Getting Job Ready with AI pilot.

Support would include using AI to search for suitable roles, tailor CVs and cover letters, prepare for interviews and understand how employers are already using digital tools in day-to-day jobs.

People will be referred onto the course through Jobcentre Plus.

The pilot forms part of a wider drive by the Department for Work and Pensions to get more people into work and help them progress once there, including reforming jobcentres into a universal careers service.

Matt O'Neill, Barnsley Council's Executive Director for Place, said the authority hoped the schemes would "make a real difference" to residents' lives.

"Tech Town is about using technology in ways that are inclusive, trusted and rooted in everyday life," he said.

"We want to make sure residents, employers and communities across the borough are ready for the jobs and services of the future."

Alongside the two new schemes, an assessment launching in autumn will look at how local charities, community groups and social enterprises are already using AI, and where further support could make the biggest difference.

Lessons from Barnsley will inform how similar approaches could be used elsewhere as the government works to equip 10 million UK workers with AI skills by 2030.

articles.title: Amazon and Flipkart have new cancellation fees for sellers and why they are unhappy with it
articles.summary: Tech News News: The story has been updated with a statement from Amazon.Online commerce platforms Amazon and Flipkart have restructured cancellation fees ahead of the.
articles.body: The story has been updated with a statement from Amazon.Online commerce platforms Amazon and Flipkart have restructured cancellation fees ahead of the festival season in the country. According to a report by PTI, Amazon India has changed the manner in which it calculates order cancellation fees for sellers using its Easy Ship and Self Ship services. As per the notice on Amazon Indiaâs seller forum, the change is effective from August 17. Similarly, Flipkart has also put in place a three-tier penalty structure for lapses in order fulfilment, effective August 23, 2026. The changes, sellers say, adds to the financial burden on small and medium enterprises already operating on thin margins, the report states.Commenting on the report, an Amazon spokesperson said : âCustomer and seller experience is at the heart of everything we do at Amazon. We expect orders placed by customers to be fulfilled reliably by sellers on our marketplace. To encourage timely and dependable fulfilment, we have revised cancellation fees for Easy Ship and Self-Ship sellers. This fee is conditional and only applies in the rare event of a seller-initiated cancellation, which accounts for less than 1% of orders on Amazon.in. We have appropriate measures in place to ensure sellers are protected when cancellations are due to circumstances beyond their control.âWhat is Amazonâs Easy Ship and Self Ship servicesUnder Self Ship, a seller on Amazon packs and delivers the product themselves, using their own courier or delivery service. No Amazon logistics are involved in self ship.As explained in the PTI report, the cancellation fee was earlier based on category-specific referral charges. But after the new change, it will now be computed as a percentage of the order value.âUnder the revised structure, sellers are charged 10% of the order value for orders below Rs 10,000, 8% for orders between Rs 10,001 and Rs 50,000, 5% for orders between Rs 50,001 and Rs 1,00,000, and 2% for orders above Rs 1,00,000, with an 18% goods and services tax levied in addition,â the report says.The cancellation fee is applicable both when a seller cancels an order for reasons other than a buyer's request, and when an order is automatically cancelled because the seller does not ship and confirm the shipment within 24 hours of the estimated ship date.Amazon to increase closing fees across its Fulfillment CenterAmazon is also increasing the closing fees across its Fulfillment Center, Easy Ship, and Seller Flex channels. According to the PTI report, the change will be effective from September 7, 2026.For those unaware, Amazon charges a closing fee every time a product is sold on its platform. The fee depends on the product's price range and the fulfillment channel used by the seller. The fee will increase by Re 1 for products priced up to Rs 500 and by Rs 3 for products priced above Rs 500. Amazon said the increase is due to rising fuel and logistics costs.What is Flipkartâs three-tier penalty structureFlipkart has introduced a three-tier penalty system for sellers who fail to meet order fulfilment deadlines. The new policy came into effect on August 23, 2026. Under the new structure, sellers will be charged Rs 30 per shipment if an order is not ready for pickup by the committed Dispatch By Date (DBD). As stated in the PTI report, a seller cancellation, or an automatic cancellation after three missed dispatch deadlines, will attract a Rs 60 penalty per shipment. If an order is delayed and later cancelled, the penalty will rise to Rs 90 per shipment.Earlier, missing a DBD deadline could lead to a seller's account being temporarily locked, which could have a bigger impact on their business. New sellers will not be covered by the policy for the first three months of their selling journey. People aware of the development told PTI that the new system aims to encourage better planning by sellers and improve the customer experience.What sellers sayAs cited in the PTI report, some sellers said that cancellations were at times caused by factors outside their control, such as delivery personnel failing to arrive for a scheduled pickup. They also questioned why cancellation fees should apply to the seller in such instances.Another seller said the difference in total fees between sellers using Amazon's fulfilment network and those on Easy Ship could be as high as Rs 45 per unit on comparable orders, which the seller claims, creates an unfair competitive situation.The PTI report quotes Vinod Kumar, Trustee of the Forum for Internet Resellers, Sellers and Traders (FIRST INDIA), who said Indian online sellers recognise the need for timely fulfilment and high customer service standards, but that the recent increase in cancellation, dispatch and other seller penalties by major e-commerce marketplaces, particularly ahead of the festive season, was a matter of concern for MSMEs already facing thin margins and rising costs."Sellers should not become the default financial shock absorbers of the e commerce ecosystem. Marketplaces must ensure transparent attribution of responsibility, reasonable and proportionate penalties, adequate advance notice of fee changes and a simple mechanism to challenge wrongful charges. The objective should be to improve fulfilment while making digital commerce more, not less, viable for small businesses," Kumar added.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: National security advisor Ajit Doval on Tuesday met Chinese vice president Han Zheng in Beijing, with the two sides discussing ways to maintain peace and tranquillity along the border and further strengthen India-China relations across economic, political and multilateral platforms.The meeting came ahead of the 25th round of special representatives talks on the India-China boundary question between Doval and Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi later on Tuesday.Sharing details of the meeting, the Embassy of India in China said, "On 25 August, NSA and Special Representative on the India-China Boundary Question, Ajit Doval called on Han Zheng, Vice President of the People's Republic of China."The embassy said Doval and Han discussed ways to strengthen peace and tranquillity in the border areas and further improve bilateral ties "across economic, political and multilateral fora", in line with the consensus reached by the leaders of the two countries.Doval arrived in Beijing on Monday for a two-day visit to participate in the Special Representatives talks with Wang Yi, who is also China's Foreign Minister.The talks are expected to focus on the boundary question, along with bilateral, regional and international issues.The Chinese Foreign Ministry has described the Special Representatives mechanism as the "main channel" for negotiations between the two countries on the boundary question and an important platform for communication on issues of mutual interest.The mechanism was established in 2003 to address the India-China boundary dispute, which stretches across roughly 3,488 km.The 24th round of talks was held in August last year, when the two sides held what Beijing described as candid and in-depth discussions and reached several common understandings.The upcoming round assumes significance as India and China seek to stabilise ties following years of tensions along the Line of Actual Control.The discussions come amid efforts by New Delhi and Beijing to gradually improve bilateral relations after the 2020 Galwan Valley clash and the prolonged military stand-off in eastern Ladakh severely strained ties.Doval and Wang had also met in June in New Delhi on the sidelines of the BRICS National Security Advisers' meeting. The Ministry of External Affairs had described those discussions as "constructive and forward-looking".MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal had said, "The two sides reviewed recent developments in bilateral relations and noted progress towards gradual normalisation. NSA underlined that stable, predictable and constructive bilateral relations contribute to building trust and better understanding between the two sides. The discussions were constructive and forward-looking."The latest talks also come amid efforts by the two countries to build on a series of high-level engagements between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping.The leaders had welcomed positive momentum and steady progress in bilateral relations during their meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin last year, after their previous meeting in Kazan in October 2024.They had reaffirmed that India and China are development partners rather than rivals and that differences should not be allowed to become disputes."A stable relationship and cooperation between India and China and their 2.8 billion peoples on the basis of mutual respect, mutual interest and mutual sensitivity are necessary for the growth and development of the two countries, as well as for a multipolar world and a multi-polar Asia befitting the trends of the 21st century," the MEA had said after the leaders' meeting.Despite the gradual improvement in ties, differences over the boundary and Arunachal Pradesh remain sensitive issues between New Delhi and Beijing.Both Doval and Wang are designated Special Representatives for the boundary talks mechanism. While the process has not resolved the long-running border dispute, officials on both sides continue to regard it as an important channel for managing tensions and maintaining communication.The talks also come ahead of Xi's expected visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit on September 12-13, which could provide an opportunity for another meeting between Xi and PM Modi and further discussions on the bilateral relationship.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: US government wants companies to pay more while filing H-1B visas, what the revised fee hike proposal says
articles.summary: Tech News News: The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has unveiled a proposal that would dramatically increase costs for employers who are sponsoring foreign w.
articles.body: The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has unveiled a proposal that would dramatically increase costs for employers who are sponsoring foreign workers under the H-1B visa program. According to the draft rule published for public inspection, companies filing cap-subject H-1B petitions would face a new standalone fee of $103,265 per petition, along with the existing charges. DHS says that the measure is aimed to recovering immigration system costs across multiple agencies.What the revised H-1b visa proposal actually saysAccording to the notice, DHS "proposes to establish a $103,265 fee, payable at the time of filing, for all H-1B cap-subject petitions, including those eligible for the advanced degree exemption, which would be imposed in addition to all other applicable fees or payments." In plain terms, this isn't a replacement for existing H-1B costs â it's a new, standalone charge stacked on top of everything employers already pay to file a petition.The fee would apply to the 65,000 visas issued under the regular annual cap as well as the 20,000 visas reserved for foreign workers holding a qualifying US master's degree or higher. It would not apply to cap-exempt petitions, which cover many roles at universities, nonprofit research organizations, and government research institutions.How DHS landed on $103,265 feeThe figure isn't arbitrary. DHS calculated it by dividing the total costs it wants to recover â $8,777,488,035 â by a projected annual filing volume of 85,000 cap-subject petitions, arriving at $103,264.57, which the agency then rounded to the nearest $5 increment consistent with its past fee-setting practice.The agency argues this approach is justified because H-1B petitioners are, in its words, an applicant pool that is "most willing and able to pay an additional fee" compared with other immigration benefit requestors, given that employers are already required to pay a certified prevailing wage to the workers they sponsor.Separate from â and stackable with â the $100,000 proclamation feeThis proposal is legally distinct from the $100,000 payment imposed last year under Presidential Proclamation 10973, which was struck down in June 2026 by a federal judge in Massachusetts (a ruling now under appeal at the First Circuit). DHS is explicit that the new $103,265 fee relies on different statutory authority â primarily sections 286(j) and (m) of the Immigration and Nationality Act â rather than the president's proclamation power used for the earlier fee.Notably, the rule states that if the proclamation's payment requirement is ever reinstated through the appeals process, employers subject to both would have to pay both amounts â the $100,000 proclamation fee and the new $103,265 rule-based fee â on top of each other. The proclamation itself is due to expire in September unless extended, and DHS notes this new rule is intended to take its place going forward.Impact on employersDHS argues that employers sponsoring Hâ1B workers generally have the resources to absorb the fee, noting median annual wages of $133,000 for Hâ1B employees. However, the government acknowledges the fee may reduce filings, particularly among smaller firms. Public comments on the proposal are open until 30 days after publication in the Federal Register (August 25, 2026).Where the money would goUnlike most past USCIS fee increases, which funded USCIS alone, this proposal spreads the roughly $8.8 billion in projected annual revenue across six federal agencies involved in different parts of the immigration system:* USCIS â 34.2% ($3.0 billion), covering adjudications, staffing increases, and IT modernization* EOIR (the Justice Department's immigration courts) â 33.7% ($2.96 billion), funding roughly 8,400 new positions including immigration judges* DOL â 13.8% ($1.21 billion), covering labor certification and wage-enforcement functions* ICE â 11.9% ($1.05 billion), covering vetting and the Student and Exchange Visitor Program* DOS â 5.5% ($484 million), covering consular vetting and fraud-prevention systems* CBP â 0.9% ($76.2 million), covering biometric entry-exit matchingDHS frames this interagency cost-sharing as consistent with its statutory authority to recover the "full costs" of administering the lawful immigration system â not just the direct cost of processing a single petition, but the broader web of vetting, enforcement, and court functions connected to it.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.summary: Tech News News: Chinese robotics company Unitreeâs CEO Wang Xingxing has predicted that humanoid robots may still be years away from reaching their own âChatGPT momen.
articles.body: Chinese robotics company Unitreeâs CEO Wang Xingxing has predicted that humanoid robots may still be years away from reaching their own âChatGPT moment.â The chief executive of the world's largest seller and manufacturer of humanoid robots has made this forecast despite growing interest in the technology. Speaking at the World Robot Conference in Beijing this week, 36-year-old Xingxing said the breakthrough could take â2 to 3 years at the fastest, and 5 or even 10 years at the slowest,â according to a translation of his speech previously reported by CNBC.Wang said robots would reach that point only when they can be placed in an unfamiliar environment or a home and complete about 80% of tasks using voice commands or text alone. His comments suggest that robots still cannot easily adapt to new situations and tasks, a limitation he said is holding back the robotics industry.Unitree CEO says robots still need years to reach ChatGPT momentWang's latest estimate is more cautious than his comments at the same conference last year, when he said the breakthrough moment for robotics would arrive within five years at the latest. His remarks also came shortly after Unitree's stock surged 460% when the company debuted on Shanghai's STAR Market.Founded by Wang about a decade ago, Unitree became more widely known last year after a video showed its humanoid robots performing a coordinated dance with humans during China's Spring Festival Gala broadcast on state television.Less than a month later, Wang was among a small group of executives seated in the front row alongside BYD chairman Wang Chuanfu and Huawei founder Ren Zhengfei at a private enterprise symposium hosted by China's president Xi Jinping in Beijing.âArtificial-intelligence-driven robots are evolving at an incredibly fast pace, surpassing my expectations. Every day brings new surprises,â Wang told China state TV following the meeting, the South China Morning Post reported.Unitree returned to the Spring Festival Gala this year, with its robots performing more advanced movements including backflips and jumps over platforms.Humanoid robots still need retraining for new tasksWang said Unitree's robots remain less efficient than human workers and need retraining for each new task. Their difficulty in adapting to unfamiliar situations remains one of the main challenges for the wider robotics industry, he said.Unitree is working on a self-evolving development loop in which its AI tests a robot's âcontrol codeâ and continuously scores the results with human help. The system is intended to improve the precision of the robots' movements, which Wang said can still go wrong in âthe last few centimetres or millimetres.âGet the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay flags off 250 new buses, including 130 electric buses
articles.summary: CHENNAI: Chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Tuesday inaugurated new bus services operated by the Metropolitan Transport Corporation (MTC) and Tamil Nadu.
articles.body: CHENNAI: Chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Tuesday inaugurated new bus services operated by the Metropolitan Transport Corporation (MTC) and Tamil Nadu State Transport Corporations at the Secretariat.He flagged off 130 low-floor electric buses worth Rs 234.5 crore and 120 other buses worth Rs 55.8 crore for public use.The 130 EV buses are from Switch Mobility, a subsidiary of Ashok Leyland and are part of Tamil Naduâs broader green mobility programme.The CM boarded one of the buses and inspected its amenities.Earlier on Monday, CM Vijay announced the expansion of the fare-free bus travel scheme for women, making services such as deluxe and express buses free for beneficiaries.Making several announcements in the Assembly, Vijay, fulfilling TVK's key electoral assurances, announced three free cooking gas cylinders and also declared that the Parandur greenfield airport project will be shelved.The project had been strongly opposed by farmers who did not wish to part with their farm lands."There will be no riders like income ceiling or number of trips for women to avail fare-free bus travel - Vettri Payanam," Vijay said, making a statement under Rule 110.Women can also travel free of charge on Express, LSS and Deluxe government buses operating in metropolitan and urban areas, as well as on regular fare buses in suburban (Mofussil) and hilly areas.The scheme will be rolled out on October 2, coinciding with Gandhi Jayanthi. Vijay said the move will entail an additional expenditure of Rs 6,000 crore per annum for the state government.On the Annapoorani Super Six scheme, a major welfare promise made by Vijay in the run-up to the April Assembly election, assuring six free LPG cylinders to every eligible family in Tamil Nadu every year to reduce household living expenses, the Chief Minister said three free cooking gas cylinders will initially be provided, with the amount credited directly into the bank accounts of beneficiaries."This will reduce the burden of the people who have been spending extra amount to obtain the cylinders. The government has decided to provide the cost of the cooking gas cylinders. Three free LPG cylinders will be given in the first phase and the price for cylinders will be directly credited into the bank accounts of the beneficiaries," Vijay said, amidst loud thumping of tables by the Treasury.The move will benefit 1,30,16,104 families with an annual income of nearly Rs 2.5 lakh, economically backward families, small and medium farmers, differently abled people and poor families."The preparatory work has commenced and the scheme will be launched this Pongal (mid-January) 2027 festival," Vijay said and added the state government will allocate Rs 4,000 crore per annum for this initiative.(With Agency Inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news. articles.title: UK to keep Russia under pressure, set up SCALP missile assembly plant in Ukraine
articles.summary: International News: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to maintain pressure on Russia despite what he described as Moscow's \"outrageous threats\", during his .
articles.body: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to maintain pressure on Russia despite what he described as Moscow's "outrageous threats", during his first official visit to Ukraine as the PM.Burnham met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", a partnership of 34 countries including Ukraine that was established by the UK and France under his predecessor Keir Starmer.The UK government has agreed to allow defence company MBDA to declassify information on British-made components used in the Scalp missile, the French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile. The move will enable Ukraine and France to work towards establishing assembly lines in Ukraine and allow Kyiv to produce the long-range weapon domestically.Scalp missiles and their UK-produced Storm Shadow variant have already been supplied to Ukraine by Britain and France and used against military targets inside Russia.Speaking during the visit, Burnham said allies were doing "everything we can" to support Ukraine, including drawing from their own air defence stocks and helping other countries do the same."This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia, the moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war," he said, while praising the "strength" of the Ukrainian people."Ukraine has been Europe's protector, not a drain on our security but the front line in keeping Europe safe," Burnham added.The comments came after Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov criticised Britain's decision to share information related to the missile's components. He said the move prevented "even the slightest progress" towards peace and claimed that the Russian military was already collecting information to identify missile production sites for destruction."Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," Peskov told reporters on Monday.Responding to the remarks, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?"Ukraine has been dependent on American supplies of Patriot air defence systems, but its stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving the country vulnerable to Russian attacks.

articles.title: Tipu Sultan cutout video with Pakistan reference sparks row in Karnataka, 23-year-old arrested
articles.summary: CHIKKAMAGALURU: Chikkamagaluru Police arrested a 23-year-old man on Tuesday for allegedly circulating a video featuring a Tipu Sultan cutout with a so.
articles.body: CHIKKAMAGALURU: Chikkamagaluru Police arrested a 23-year-old man on Tuesday for allegedly circulating a video featuring a Tipu Sultan cutout with a song containing references to âPakistanâ and âMujahidâ, prompting heightened security in the district, police said.Superintendent of Police Jitendra Kumar Dayama clarified that the action was not related to the installation of the Tipu Sultan cutout itself.He said a similar cutout had been installed at Tipunagara at the same location, around the same time and with the same dimensions in previous years.According to Dayama, police had earlier told organisers they could continue with arrangements followed over the past five to 10 years, but would not permit any new cutouts or decorations.The issue surfaced around 5pm to 5.30pm when the cutout was used as the backdrop in a video and a song containing a word referring to âPakistanâ and âMujahidâ was added, the SP said.The video was later circulated through multiple social media accounts and came to the policeâs attention, ANI reported.Police registered an FIR under Sections 196 and 299 and traced the account that first circulated the video, following which the 23-year-old local resident of Tipunagara was arrested and is being produced before a magistrate, Dayama said.He allegedly shared the video as his WhatsApp status, sent direct messages to some Instagram accounts and other individuals, and uploaded a reel on his Instagram account, police said.Police are also probing the role of others who may have viewed, shared or recirculated the content."We are still in the process of ascertaining their role. If someone else also with intention did the same, then we will definitely arrest them and produce them," Dayama said.The SP said police were also trying to identify the person who originally created the video. A request has been sent to Meta for the relevant IP address as part of efforts to trace the original account.Dayama said the situation in Chikkamagaluru remained peaceful and police had spoken to community leaders. He said action would be taken against anyone attempting to create disturbances.Police social media monitoring teams at both the district and police station levels were also closely monitoring the situation, he said.More than 300 Home Guards, four Karnataka State Reserve Police (KSRP) platoons and local police personnel have been deployed for security, Dayama said. The forces will continue to monitor the situation during the function and the upcoming procession."Everything is peaceful, everything is calm, and this function will go on," Dayama said.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: Blood Moon partial lunar eclipse: How and when to see it in UK skies
articles.summary: There will be a partial lunar eclipse in the UK on 28 August, and may cause the Moon appear reddish in colour.
articles.body:
Skywatchers across the UK could have the chance to see a stunning partial lunar eclipse later this week as the Sun, Earth, and Moon line up in the night sky.

Lunar eclipses occur when the Moon is full which will take place in the early hours of 28 August. It may cause the full Moon - nicknamed the Sturgeon Moon - to take on an eerie reddish glow.

It comes just weeks after the UK experienced its most dramatic partial solar eclipse in nearly 30 years.

Adding to the spectacle, its position in the sky will be low on the horizon, causing a phenomenon known as the Moon illusion. This makes the Moon appear bigger and more dramatic than usual.

How and when can I see the partial lunar eclipse in the UK?

The eclipse will take place in the early hours of Friday 28 August.

The partial eclipse will begin at 03:33 BST in London, when the Moon enters Earth's darkest shadow.

It will reach its maximum at 05:12 BST, when around 90% of the Moon will be within the umbra.

By this point the Moon will be very low in the south-western sky, causing something known as the Moon illusion .

This is a term for when the Moon appears much larger than it is based on its position in the sky - an effect caused by the way our brains process visual information.

The effect is particularly noticeable during a moonrise or moonset, when the lunar disc is seen alongside familiar objects on the ground.

Exact moonset times will vary across the UK.

In London, it will set and move out of sight at approximately 06:15 BST.

A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, causing the Moon to temporarily move into the Earth's shadow.

During a partial eclipse, only part of the Moon enters the darkest section of that shadow, known as the umbra.

The Moon is not completely cut off from sunlight, however.

Sunlight passing through the Earth's atmosphere is scattered, with shorter blue wavelengths scattering more easily, while more of the longer wavelength red light reach the Moon.

These wavelengths are then reflected back towards Earth, giving the eclipsed Moon its reddish colour.

What is the weather forecast for the Blood Moon lunar eclipse?

For the best chance of seeing the eclipse, astronomers recommend finding a high location with an unobstructed view towards the south-western horizon.

Clear skies will, of course, be essential.

Viewing conditions are expected to vary considerably across the UK during the early hours of Friday morning.

With low pressure in charge, cloud and heavy showers are likely to affect some parts of the country, while other areas remain clear.

Currently, the best viewing conditions are expected across central and eastern parts of England and Wales. However, even here, the cloud cover could change a lot from one hour to the next and is very hard to forecast accurately.

You can check the latest hour-by-hour forecast where you are online or via the BBC Weather app.

articles.title: No longer safe at the rear? How Chinaâs hypersonic weapons could hunt US support aircraft
articles.summary: International News: China has developed hypersonic glide vehicles that can launch air-to-air missiles, a new capability that could threaten high-value US aircraft such as.
articles.body: China has developed hypersonic glide vehicles that can launch air-to-air missiles, a new capability that could threaten high-value US aircraft such as command-and-control and surveillance planes from thousands of miles away, according to Bloomberg.The development is part of Chinaâs wider effort to expand the use of its huge missile arsenal for different military missions. A person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg that China has also added air-to-air capabilities to some hypersonic cruise missiles and anti-ship capabilities to several other missile types.Hypersonic weapons could target support aircraftUS military aircraft such as aerial tankers, airborne warning-and-control planes and flying command posts are designed to stay away from the main battlefield. But the new Chinese weapons could put even these aircraft at risk.A hypersonic glide vehicle launched by a DF-17 missile could travel about 1,500 miles (2,414 km), a distance just short of the route from China to the US territory of Guam, a major American military base.Chinaâs DF-27 missile has an estimated range of about 5,000 miles, putting Hawaii within its reach.Hypersonic glide vehicles, or HGVs, are warheads that can move and change direction while travelling through the atmosphere. This makes them harder to track and intercept than traditional ballistic missiles.No other country is publicly known to operate a weapon that combines an HGV with air-to-air missiles.A report by the US air forceâs China Aerospace Studies Institute this year said that Chinaâs missile modernisation efforts âincreasingly prioritize the ability to inflict coordinated, systemâlevel damage across an adversaryâs operational architecture.âWeapon has major challengesDespite the threat, using a ballistic missile to attack an aircraft thousands of miles away would not be simple.At maximum range, a ballistic missile could take 20 minutes or more to reach its target. This means the missile would need highly accurate and constantly updated information about the aircraftâs location.The process of collecting information from distant sensors and passing it to the missile creates a long âkill chainâ, which an enemy could potentially disrupt.There is another major risk. A ballistic missile launch could be mistaken for a nuclear attack. This âdiscrimination problemâ could make the weapon especially dangerous during a major conflict, as an opponent might misinterpret the launch and respond with nuclear weapons.China expands missile arsenalChina appears to have sharply increased missile production in recent years. Bloomberg reported in May that Chinese missile production rose at the fastest pace since Xi Jinping became president in 2013, based on its analysis of the sectorâs finances.Chinaâs long-range PL-15 air-to-air missile has already been used in combat. The missile featured during last yearâs brief conflict between India and Pakistan, with Pakistan saying it used the weapons to shoot down several Indian aircraft.The Pentagon estimated that China had at least 3,150 ballistic missiles and 300 ground-launched cruise missiles as of 2024. Those figures represented increases of 147% and 50%, respectively, from 2015, when the US began publicly disclosing such estimates.US also develops longer-range missilesLong-range air-to-air missiles are considered important for any future major conflict.The US has developed the AIM-174B from RTX Corp.âs SM-6 air defence missile. Its exact range is classified, although the ground-launched SM-6 can travel 250 miles or more.On Saturday, the US Navy said it was testing the AIM-424 Malice air-to-air missile made by RTX unit Raytheon Co. The missile has a range of more than 300 miles, according to the Navy.Lockheed Martin Corp.âs AIM-260 is also in production but has not yet entered service. It is expected to have a very long range.In Europe, MBDA Missile Systems Services SASâ Meteor is widely used. The ramjet-powered missile can strike targets more than 100 miles away.

articles.title: Looking to improve your TV's picture quality? These 5 setting changes can help
articles.summary: Tech News News: Many people spend hours watching movies, shows and sports on their TV, but only a few make the most of their screenâs picture quality. The good news i.
articles.body: Many people spend hours watching movies, shows and sports on their TV, but only a few make the most of their screenâs picture quality. The good news is that users do not need expensive equipment or professional calibration to improve their TV picture. A few simple changes to picture mode, brightness, motion settings and sharpness can make movies, shows and sports look more natural and detailed. Here are some of the most important TV settings to change for better picture quality.Start with the right picture modeThe first setting to check is Picture Mode. Most TVs offer options such as Standard, Vivid, Dynamic, Sports, Movie, Cinema and Filmmaker Mode. These modes generally aim for a more accurate and natural-looking image. Filmmaker Mode, where available, also reduces extra picture processing. Vivid and Dynamic modes may look eye-catching, but they can push brightness and colours too far for regular viewing.Turn off motion smoothing for moviesIf movies look unusually smooth, almost like a soap opera or live television, motion smoothing could be the reason. This feature adds extra frames to make movement appear smoother.Motion processing can be useful in some situations, but many viewers prefer to switch it off or lower it when watching films. It might be called MotionFlow or Picture Clarity, depending on the brand of your TV.Carefully adjust brightness and contrastThe brightness and contrast can make a big difference to what you see on screen. Contrast affects highlights and bright areas, while brightness or black level setting affects how much detail is visible in dark scenes.A good approach is to use a familiar movie or show with both dark and bright scenes.Don't increase sharpness too muchMore sharpness does not always mean more detail in the picture quality. Instead, it can add artificial outlines around objects and make the image look unnatural. Hence, it is recommended to lower the sharpness setting. Having said that the best level can vary by TV and personal preference.Check energy-saving and automatic brightnessSome TVs automatically adjust screen brightness depending on the room lighting or energy-saving settings. While these features can help in reducing power consumption, they may also make the picture look dim.If the screen appears inconsistent, checking features such as ambient light sensors, adaptive brightness or energy-saving modes may help. articles.summary: Tech News News: Goldman Sachs has cautioned that Americaâs energy sector is facing a âbig troubleâ not only from the power supply constraints but also from the loomin.
articles.body: Goldman Sachs has cautioned that Americaâs energy sector is facing a âbig troubleâ not only from the power supply constraints but also from the looming labour shortage. According to a report by Fortune, the investment bankâs latest report estimates that the US power and grid value chain will require around 500,000 additional workers by 2030 to meet demand. With roles often requiring three to four years of training, the sector faces a significant skills gap. The report also highlights that the energy apprenticeship pipeline had just 45,000 entrants in 2024, which is far short of the 65,000 professionals needed annually to close the labor supply gap. Rising demand for AI infrastructure, which requires even greater power capacity, could widen the shortage further. Goldman Sachs noted: âPower is a critical bottleneckâbut increasingly, the requisite labor presents a structural constraint of its own.âGoldman Sachs points to humanoid robots and autonomous equipmentGoldman Sachs believes that as the workforce is not able to keep pace, the companies would require humanoids and other autonomous equipements as the potential solution. The firm also believes that the humanoid robot market will witness growth and will reach 1.4 million by 2035 increasing from 20,000 in 2025. This decrease in the human workforce will offer 6,900% increase to the humanoid market. Companies such as Tesla, Amazon, and Caterpillar are already deploying autonomous systems, while China has begun using robots for power grid inspection and maintenance.Goldman Sachs is 'very impressed' with MicrosoftRecently, Microsoft offered Wall Street its clearest signal yet that its massive capital commitments to artificial intelligence are yielding tangible, diversified revenue streams. The performance sparked a historic rally in the software giantâs equity, driving its sharpest single-day gain in nearly 18 years. The catalyst came as Microsoft reported its fastest acceleration in cloud revenue since 2022. The results demonstrated that its core Azure infrastructure and enterprise AI offerings are expanding rapidly among corporate clients, while management simultaneously signaled a moderation in capital expenditure growthâaddressing a key area of investor anxiety over margin compression.In an interview on Bloomberg Television, Goldman Sachs Group managing director and senior equity research analyst Gabriela Borges highlighted the shift in market sentiment. âYouâre seeing more breadcrumbs around Microsoftâs ability to pull varying levers on the monetization side that perhaps were not nearly as obvious as before,â Borges said. Following the quarterly report, Borges reiterated her Buy rating on Microsoft while raising her 12-month price target nearly 5% to $640, implying a potential upside of approximately 64% from Wednesdayâs closing price. During intraday trading in New York on Thursday, Microsoft shares surged 17% to $457 -- positioning the company for its largest single-day percentage gain since October 2008.At the earnings call, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said that the company now counted more than 30 million paid users of Microsoft 365 Copilot, the AI assistant sold as an add-on to the ubiquitous Office software.
