articles.title: Nathan Cofnas, scholar who exposed Jason Ardayâs plagiarism, says he had no ill will towards him: âThis was about DEIâ
articles.summary: UK News: Nathan Cofnas, the American researcher who first publicly detailed extensive plagiarism allegations against Cambridge Universityâs youngest Black prof.
articles.body: Nathan Cofnas, the American researcher who first publicly detailed extensive plagiarism allegations against Cambridge University’s youngest Black professor, Jason Arday, has said he bore no personal animosity towards the late academic. In his first detailed comments to VRT NWS after Arday’s death, Cofnas stated that he “had zero interest” in Arday as an individual and “no ill will towards him”. He insisted the controversy was fundamentally about diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies at Cambridge and similar institutions. “I set in motion a series of events that led to a tragic outcome, but this was about diversity policy and Cambridge. Arday played only a supporting role in it,” Cofnas said. He added that he had wanted Arday to remain a professor and “live his best life”.Nathan Cofnas challenges the story behind Jason Arday’s rise at CambridgeIn March 2023, Jason Arday was appointed professor of sociology of education at the University of Cambridge, becoming the institution’s youngest Black professor, and his appointment attracted widespread positive coverage. Central to that coverage was Arday’s account of overcoming extraordinary challenges in his youth. He said he had been diagnosed with autism, global developmental delay, mutism, deafness and dyscalculia, had remained non-verbal until the age of 11 and had only learned to read and write at 18. He also spoke publicly about surviving epilepsy, testicular cancer and a brain tumour. His story of overcoming these difficulties and rising into academia was widely presented as an example of exceptional resilience. However, subsequent scrutiny by The Guardian found that questions extended beyond the allegations concerning his research. Several claims about his academic career and qualifications could not be substantiated. Arday’s biography at Jesus College, Cambridge, stated that he had held visiting professorships at Ohio State University and the University of Glasgow, but Ohio State said he had never been employed there, while Glasgow also denied that he had held the claimed visiting professorship. His biography also described him as an honorary professor at Durham University, although the university said he no longer held any role there. Arday had further stated that he completed a master’s degree in psychodynamic practices at Birkbeck, University of London, and subsequently became a fully qualified counsellor, but Birkbeck told The Guardian that it could not find a record of a student named Jason Arday having studied there.His claim to have authored a book with Palgrave Macmillan was also questioned, with the publisher confirming that it had received a proposal but that the book was never published. These findings became significant because they concerned not merely interpretations of his achievements but specific claims about institutional affiliations, qualifications and publications that could be checked against the records of the organisations named. The scrutiny later expanded to his athletic and charitable claims, including his statements about running 30 marathons in 35 days, completing 600 miles in six days and raising £5 million or more for charity. The Guardian reported that some institutional descriptions of the 600-mile challenge were subsequently amended, while Arday clarified that the feat had actually taken place over 12 days because rest days had been included.The plagiarism allegationsIn mid-July 2026, Nathan Cofnas, a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University who describes himself as a “racial realist” and critic of DEI policies, published a Substack article titled “DEI Fraud and Cover-Up at Cambridge”. Using plagiarism-detection software, Cofnas argued that numerous passages in Arday’s doctoral thesis and later academic work had been taken from other sources with minimal alteration. He presented the case as evidence of deeper problems with how universities prioritise identity in appointments.The Substack post triggered intense coverage, particularly in British newspapers. Cambridge announced an investigation on 5 August 2026 into Arday’s academic qualifications and honorary appointments. The same day, Arday resigned, stating that the pressure had become too great for his well-being and family, while emphasising that his departure was not an admission of guilt. A week later, on 14 August, Arday was found dead at his home in London at the age of 41. Many on social media and some commentators attributed responsibility for the outcome to Cofnas and the ensuing scrutiny. There is, however, no established evidence in the material provided that Cofnas caused Arday’s death.Cofnas’s response and suspensionSpeaking to VRT NWS, Cofnas acknowledged that his actions set events in motion that ended tragically. He argued, however, that powerful people must remain open to criticism even when it risks causing personal distress. “You have to be able to criticise such people, even if there is a risk that they will misunderstand it or feel very bad about it,” he said. Shortly after Arday’s death, Ghent University suspended Cofnas preventively and opened a preliminary disciplinary investigation, stating that it took his public statements “very seriously”.Broader controversyCofnas remains a polarising figure. He has previously argued that genetic factors play a non-trivial role in average group differences in intelligence, views that contributed to the end of his association with Emmanuel College, Cambridge, in 2024. Supporters see his work on Arday as a necessary defence of academic standards; critics describe it as racially motivated. In the same VRT interview, Cofnas characterised an earlier on-camera remark about heading a future “Department of Eugenics and Race Science at Harvard” as a joke based on his belief that universities should study race and hereditary influences more openly.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1912, New Zealand released wallabies near Rotorua; they now occupy more than 200,000 hectares and, if left unchecked, could spread across a third of the country by 2065, causing $84 million in damage a year
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Wallabies introduced to New Zealand more than a century ago have spread across more than 200,000 hectares in the countryâs North Island. Authorities a.
articles.body: Wallabies introduced to New Zealand more than a century ago have spread across more than 200,000 hectares in the countryâs North Island. Authorities are now working to control their population because the animals can damage native forests, compete with farm animals for pasture and harm young trees in plantations.A wallaby is a small or middle-sized macropod native to Australia and New Guinea The wallabies in the Bay of Plenty region were brought from Australia. According to Bay of Plenty region of New Zealandâs North Island, Dama and parma wallabies were introduced to Kawau Island by former Prime Minister of New Zealand Sir George Grey around 1870, along with animals including monkeys, zebra and gnu. In 1912, dama wallabies from Kawau Island were released near Lake Okareka in the Bay of Plenty.Since then, the animals have established themselves across a large area. The Bay of Plenty Regional Council says they are now found across more than 200,000 hectares. Their current range stretches from Rotorua east to Kawerau, and south beyond Maunga Kakaramea, also known as Rainbow Mountain, towards the Paeroa Range between Reporoa and Waikite Valley.The spread is a concern because wallabies are difficult to detect. They are cautious and mainly active at night. During the day, they often shelter in dense forest or scrub. They can live in both native and exotic forests, particularly in places where forest is close to pasture or open, sunny areas.Wallabies can change forestsThe main concern is what the animals eat. Wallabies feed on native tree seedlings, ferns and grasses. If this feeding continues over a long period, it can prevent some native plants from growing and replacing older trees.This can gradually change the structure and composition of native forests. Some plants eaten selectively by wallabies are also important food sources for native birds and other wildlife.Wallabies can also cause problems outside native forests. In exotic plantations, they can damage young pine and eucalyptus seedlings. On farms, they compete with livestock for pasture, reducing the amount of food available to farm animals.The animals prefer areas where they can move between forest cover and open land. They often gather in small family groups. Their spread has been slowed in some places by natural barriers such as lakes and rivers. However, authorities say people have sometimes helped wallabies move beyond these barriers.Wallabies can spread quicklyWallabies are highly mobile and estimates their populations can spread by up to 2 kilometres a year on average. If their spread is not controlled, scientists estimate, they could eventually occupy one-third of New Zealand by 2065. Government estimates that the damage caused by wallabies could reach $84 million a year if they are left unchecked. It also says the cost of the damage is expected to increase each year.Wallabies have therefore been classified as an unwanted organism under New Zealandâs Biosecurity Act 1993. According to the law, Wallabies cannot be bred, sold, moved or exhibited without a permit.Effort to controlThe Bay of Plenty Regional Council has different management categories for wallaby species. Dama and parma wallabies are covered by eradication and progressive containment programmes.Under the eradication programme, pests are present but limited enough in their size or distribution for removal to be considered possible and cost-effective. Progressive containment is used where the aim is to stop the pest from spreading, reduce its distribution or remove it from parts of the region over time.Three other wallaby species Bennettâs wallaby, brush-tailed rock wallaby and swamp wallaby are not currently known to be established in the Bay of Plenty. These species are listed under an exclusion programme, which means the Regional Council is responsible for managing new incursions into the region.Night shooting and poisoning One method used on private farmland is night shooting. Wallabies are mostly active at night, making this approach suitable for controlling them in areas where it can be carried out safely.The Bay of Plenty Regional Council says night shooting should only be attempted by licensed and experienced shooters. It also says accurate bullet placement is essential for humane kills.Poisoning is another control option, although only limited pesticides are registered for use against wallabies. The council lists 1080 and Feratox encapsulated cyanide as the two registered pesticides.Their use is regulated, and handlers must hold a Controlled Substances Licence. The use of these pesticides is also subject to requirements from WorkSafe and the Medical Officer of Health.Wallabies can be vulnerable to aerial or hand-broadcast bait, but they do not always use bait stations. The report notes that where wallabies live alongside possums, the smaller but more aggressive possums can prevent wallabies from reaching some bait stations.People are asked to report wallabies whether they are alive or dead. Their tracks and droppings can also provide evidence of their presence.A wallaby footprint has a distinctive shape. The long hind feet can leave tracks in sand or soft soil, with a large central toe extending beyond the outer toe. Their droppings are also distinctive and are slightly larger than individual deer pellets, often with a tear-drop shape.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Bangladesh-India reset stalls over Hasina: What would break the deadlock?
articles.summary: Analysts say an Indian commitment not to allow ousted Bangladesh PM to engage in politics from their soil would help.
articles.body:
Dhaka, Bangladesh — New Delhi and Dhaka had been quietly planning Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s first visit to India since taking office earlier this year, when a news conference shattered those efforts.

Former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina, convicted of crimes against humanity in her country, addressed a news conference held in the heart of the Indian capital by video on August 5, where she, her son and their Awami League party colleagues criticised the mass uprising that had brought her down.

Bangladesh responded swiftly, saying it was “outraged” that Hasina had been allowed to speak publicly from Indian soil, where she has been in exile since her ouster in August 2024. Dhaka had specifically warned New Delhi against allowing political activities that could affect bilateral relations.

Bangladesh subsequently said a “propitious environment” was needed before the trip, while asking New Delhi to act on extradition requests involving Hasina and other fugitives.

India says the requests remain “under examination” through established procedures.

But interviews with Bangladeshi officials and analysts suggest the immediate dispute may be more nuanced than a simple extradition standoff.

The key question may be less when India hands Hasina over than what India allows her to do while she remains there.

Faisal Mahmud, a former press minister at the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi, said extradition and Hasina’s political activities should be treated as separate issues.

“The stalemate between Bangladesh and India stems largely from New Delhi giving Sheikh Hasina a literal megaphone while she remains in exile there – something Dhaka had specifically asked India not to allow,” Mahmud told Al Jazeera.

Extradition, he said, was “an entirely different matter, and a far more complicated and lengthy one” that the Rahman government understood.

“At this point, the impasse over Tarique’s proposed visit to India, and over any broader reset of the frosty bilateral relationship, is not centred on Hasina’s extradition,” Mahmud said. “It is centred on India allowing her to conduct political activities from its soil.”

That concern predates the government under Rahman’s Bangladesh Nationalist Party.

During an April 4, 2025 meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, then head of Bangladesh’s interim administration, asked New Delhi to prevent Hasina from making what he described as “incendiary statements” from Indian soil.

Humaiun Kobir, deputy head of Bangladesh’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, told Al Jazeera that Dhaka wanted “a good and working relationship with India based on trust and mutual respect”.

“But letting terrorists like Sheikh Hasina destabilise our country from India is not acceptable,” Kobir said, using the government’s description of the former prime minister.

He argued that relations could enter “a new phase” if the leadership of both countries wanted it, but said New Delhi must recognise Bangladesh’s changed political reality following the 2024 uprising.

“No one can conduct any terror activity from a sovereign land,” Kobir said. “It is unacceptable that the terrorists who killed our people are allowed to talk from their land and incite violence in Bangladesh.”

He said Dhaka wanted India to return other Bangladeshis accused of crimes, including suspects in the killing of Sharif Osman Hadi, an outspoken critic of Hasina and India who was murdered in 2025. His alleged killers were subsequently arrested by India, where they had crossed over.

Yet Kobir’s comments also suggest Dhaka does not want the Hasina dispute to indefinitely prevent high-level engagement.

Talks over Rahman’s visit remain under way, he said, describing a meeting between the Bangladeshi and Indian prime ministers as ultimately unavoidable. Over the weekend, in fact, India’s Rashtrapati Bhavan — the presidential palace — issued a notice suggesting that it was preparing to host Rahman, only to withdraw the document hours later.

“A meeting is a must,” Kobir told Al Jazeera. “But only when it aligns with our national interest.”

“It can be next week, two weeks later or two months later,” he added.

That distinction matters because restricting Hasina’s political activity and extraditing her present very different challenges for New Delhi.

Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia by Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal after being convicted of crimes against humanity over the deadly crackdown on the 2024 uprising. She rejects the proceedings as politically motivated.

Bangladesh first formally sought Hasina’s extradition on December 23, 2024, through a diplomatic note sent under the countries’ 2013 extradition treaty.

After her death sentence in November 2025, Dhaka reiterated the request, and India subsequently said it was “under examination”.

On August 11, India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said Bangladesh’s request for Sheikh Hasina’s extradition was being examined under India’s “established procedures”, adding that New Delhi would share an update when there was further progress.

The MEA did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for further details on the matter.

Pinak Ranjan Chakravarty, a former Indian high commissioner to Bangladesh, said the matter must proceed through treaty provisions and India’s legal system.

“All legal formalities have to be completed for obtaining a judicial order for extradition,” Chakravarty told Al Jazeera.

He said the treaty also contained grounds under which extradition could be refused.

Some analysts see a political contradiction in the extradition demand.

David Bergman, a veteran observer of Bangladesh politics, argues that Dhaka is pressing India to return Hasina while potentially preferring that she remain outside the country.

“Bangladesh demands extradition knowing that the Indian government will never extradite Hasina,” Bergman told Al Jazeera, adding: “It is apparently playing to the gallery of Bangladesh public opinion.”

“At the same time, the government does not actually want Hasina to return,” Bergman said, referring to a dilemma that other analysts too have pointed to: Hasina’s return could create as many political and legal problems for Dhaka as it resolves.

Bangladesh would have custody of a former prime minister sentenced to death, forcing the government to confront the politically and internationally sensitive consequences of imprisoning, and potentially executing, one of the country’s most consequential political figures.

But the Hasina question is only one part of a broader recalibration of Dhaka’s relationship with New Delhi.

Shahab Enam Khan, professor of international relations at Jahangirnagar University, said Dhaka’s current posture should not be read simply as anti-India. Khan told Al Jazeera that Bangladesh still needs trade, defence, security and people-to-people ties with India.

He said the government’s stance reflects two pressures: asserting Bangladesh’s legal and sovereign authority, and responding to public sentiment shaped by what he described as New Delhi’s close alignment with Hasina’s Awami League over the past two decades.

Khan argued that India had invested heavily in the Awami League as its principal political partner in Bangladesh and had been slow to fully adjust to the country’s post-2024 political reality.

He said New Delhi was now “increasingly embracing the political reality in Bangladesh”, but added that Dhaka needed to see that shift translated into concrete outcomes.

The political dispute has not halted practical engagement.

A Confederation of Indian Industry delegation visited Dhaka this month for talks with ministers and business leaders even as uncertainty over Rahman’s proposed India visit intensified. Bilateral merchandise trade remains above $12bn annually, with India exporting $10.56bn worth of goods to Bangladesh, according to the Indian High Commission in Dhaka.

For former Indian High Commissioner Chakravarty, that reflects an unavoidable structural reality.

“Geography is an immutable factor in geopolitics,” he told Al Jazeera. “It binds India and Bangladesh in a manner that cannot be ignored by policymakers in both countries.”

But he criticised Dhaka for attaching conditions to Rahman’s visit.

“I do not think that the larger national interest and bilateral ties should be held hostage to any individual,” Chakravarty said.

Sreeradha Datta, a professor specialising in South Asian studies at India’s OP Jindal Global University, pointed to another dimension of that interdependence: Bangladesh’s attempts to diversify its external relationships have not reduced India’s strategic importance.

She said Dhaka’s expanding engagement with the United States and China, growing defence cooperation with Turkiye and renewed outreach to Pakistan have added to New Delhi’s concerns about Bangladesh’s foreign policy direction.

China has become particularly important, Datta said, with Beijing’s sustained economic and strategic engagement giving it a growing role in Bangladesh’s development and foreign policy calculations.

Even so, she argued, Bangladesh’s broader external partnerships cannot diminish India’s structural importance.

“Neither side can stay disengaged for long,” Datta told Al Jazeera, noting that geography ensures India will remain strategically important to Bangladesh.

The two countries share a 4,096km (2,546-mile) land border.

Datta said Bangladesh also occupies a critical place in India’s eastern connectivity, security and neighbourhood strategy, adding that the relationship is supported by more than 70 bilateral mechanisms.

That structural dependence also helps explain why, despite the political standoff, New Delhi has stopped short of closing the door on high-level engagement.

As recently as August 18, the MEA said Rahman’s invitation remained open, while reiterating that New Delhi wants a “positive, constructive and forward-looking” relationship with Bangladesh based on mutual interest and reciprocity.

The unresolved question is what concession, public or private, could create enough political space for both governments to move towards a meeting without appearing to have backed down.

articles.title: In 1952, a retired Canadian undertaker began saving empty embalming-fluid bottles: Around 500,000 bottles and 250 tons of glass later, he had built a castle-like home
articles.summary: Rest of World News: David H. Brown retired from the funeral business in 1952 after 35 years as an undertaker, when he began collecting empty bottles that had once held em.
articles.body: David H. Brown retired from the funeral business in 1952 after 35 years as an undertaker, when he began collecting empty bottles that had once held embalming fluid. Brown believed the square glass containers could have another use, and over time, that idea grew into a full-scale construction project on the shores of Kootenay Lake in British Columbia, Canada. The result was a two-story home built with around 500,000 discarded embalming-fluid bottles, with a castle-like front and a cloverleaf-shaped layout.The story of the house is documented by SPACES Archives, which records that Brown began the project in 1952. The archive describes the structure as having the footprint of a three-leaf clover, while crenellations across the front gave it an appearance more associated with a small castle than a conventional retirement home. The bottles had previously been used to hold formaldehyde embalming fluid in Brown's own profession and were collected from undertakers and funeral-industry colleagues.He collected bottles from funeral homes across western CanadaKootenay Rockies Tourism says that Brown traveled across western Canada to collect bottles from friends in the funeral profession, and eventually, he had acquired about 500,000 square-shaped embalming-fluid bottles. Together, the glass reportedly weighed around 250 tons. Brown's used the bottles as a building material, and Kootenay Rockies Tourism quotes him as saying the project began because he wanted to "indulge a whim of a peculiar nature." The same account says Brown had concluded that the discarded bottles should have some practical use after he retired.The containers were square, which allowed them to be arranged more easily than ordinary round bottles. SPACES Archives explains that they were laid horizontally, and their mouths and necks were pointed inward. Their square bottoms formed the outside surface of the house. Wood lath was wired between the bottle necks to hold the arrangement in place, while cedar planking formed the interior walls, and the building was therefore more than a collection of bottles embedded in concrete. Brown developed a structure around the glass and incorporated it into the walls themselves. Kootenay Rockies Tourism.The bottle collection became a 1,200-square-foot houseThe finished building measured roughly 48 feet long and 24 feet wide, with about 1,200 square feet of floor space. SPACES Archives records six round rooms, including a full kitchen, two bedrooms and a fireplace. It was two stories high, and the walls were made from hundreds of thousands of glass bottles, while the facade had crenellations resembling the upper edges of a castle wall. The surrounding property also became part of Brown's larger project. A wishing well, waterwheel, bridge, stone walls and other smaller structures were added to the grounds. Kootenay Rockies Tourism also describes a glass-bottle bridge and a path leading toward the lakeshore.Brown and his wife had originally intended to use the building as their private residence, and that changed as people traveling along Highway 3A near Boswell began stopping to see it. SPACES Archives says the Browns eventually decided to open the property to visitors rather than keep it solely as a home. It stands near Kootenay Lake, south of Boswell in southeastern British Columbia. The house remains one of the more unusual examples of reuse architecture in the region because of the scale of Brown's collection and the specific source of the containers.The house is still standing more than seven decades laterThe Glass House still exists at 11341 Highway 3A even seventy years after its construction began. SPACES Archives lists its status as "Extant," which means that the structure remains standing, while current regional tourism listings continue to advertise it as a visitor attraction. The Kootenay Lake Chamber of Commerce currently lists the Glass House as open for paid tours seven days a week from May through October. Its listing identifies the property as being made from more than half a million embalming-fluid bottles and provides the same Highway 3A location near Boswell.It began in 1952 as a retired undertaker's attempt to find another use for empty bottles and ended with a house made from about 250 tons of glass. The building was never hidden away as a private curiosity, and drivers still stop along the Kootenay Lake route to see the bottle walls, the cloverleaf-shaped structure and the former funeral-industry containers that Brown turned into a home.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Global ocean temperatures hit record high as El Nino intensifies
articles.summary: Copernicus warns of ‘unprecedented strain’ on world’s oceans as El Nino and climate change drive up sea temperatures.
articles.body:
The average global sea surface temperature has reached its highest level on record, a European Union agency said, warning that a rapidly intensifying El Nino and human-caused climate change were putting “unprecedented strain” on the world’s oceans.

In a statement on Monday, the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service said sea surface temperatures hit 21.1 degrees Celsius (69.98 degrees Fahrenheit) on Friday and Saturday, surpassing the previous record of 21.09C (69.96F) set in March 2024.

“This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress,” said Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). “El Nino is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming.”

Copernicus called the timing of the new record “particularly notable”. It said global ocean temperatures usually peak in March and April, when the summer in the Southern Hemisphere – which is mostly ocean – draws to a close.

But this year, the record was set in August.

Burgess told The Associated Press news agency that the oceans will keep getting hotter until the current El Nino – a natural temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that then warps weather and raises temperatures globally – reaches its peak, which is expected sometime between November and January.

The World Meteorological Organization, too, said it expects El Nino to strengthen in the coming months, and Copernicus said its seasonal forecasting system indicates that the event “could reach levels not seen for several decades”.

The added heat from El Nino comes as long-term fossil-fuel-driven warming has already raised ocean temperatures by 0.8C (1.44F), Burgess noted.

Copernicus also warned that rising ocean temperatures have “far-reaching consequences” for marine ecosystems and coastal communities.

Warmer oceans contribute to sea-level rise through thermal expansion, it said, and increase the likelihood and intensity of marine heatwaves, which can damage coral reefs and seagrass beds. This can in turn disrupt food chains and threaten industries such as fishing and aquaculture.

Warmer oceans are less able to absorb carbon dioxide, too, it said, weakening one of the planet’s key defences against climate change.

Higher ocean temperatures can also supply more heat and moisture to the atmosphere, enhancing the “potential for extreme weather events”.

Jane Lubchenco, an oceanographer and former head of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, called the finding “very troubling”.

“An ocean this warm destabilises weather patterns and threatens food security, economic prosperity and marine life,” Lubchenco told the AP. “A warmer ocean is not our friend.”

articles.title: Rescuers find no trace of 22 missing crew days after cargo ship sinks in Bay of Bengal
articles.summary: Rescuers searching for 22 missing sailors have found no trace of their Panama-flagged cargo ship after the vessel sank in the Bay of Bengal last week, the In...
articles.body:
NEW DELHI (AP) — Rescuers searching for 22 missing sailors have found no trace of their Panama-flagged cargo ship after the vessel sank in the Bay of Bengal last week, the Indian Coast Guard said Tuesday.

Search aircraft and ships on Tuesday were scouring the area where the cargo ship MV Ocean Winner reportedly sunk Saturday about 276 miles (444 kilometers) from the Paradip coast of India's eastern Odisha state.

The joint search by the Indian Coast Guard and Indian Navy has been complicated by the area's exceptionally deep waters and found only an oil slick and two life rafts near the vessel's last known position, officials said.

The lack of wreckage has hampered efforts to determine the cause of the sinking and where to focus search operations, authorities said.

The vessel transporting iron ore to China was carrying 24 crew members, including 20 Chinese nationals, three Myanmar nationals and one Bangladeshi, according to the coast guard.

Two Chinese crew members were rescued Saturday following a distress call from the ship, the coast guard said.

articles.title: In 1999, the Azores protected forest for the endangered Azores bullfinch; two decades of restoration later, surveys estimated about 1,300 birds in suitable habitat
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how dedicated conservation efforts have helped restore the Azores bullfinch population from 100 pairs in 1999 to over 1,300 individuals today by revitalizing their habitat in the Azores.
articles.body: In 1999, the Azores set aside the Pico da Vara/Ribeira do Guilherme region on SÃ£o Miguel Island for the conservation of the endangered Azores bullfinch, a bird found nowhere else in the world. At the time, the bird species had been reduced to around 100 breeding pairs and survived in a small remnant of native laurel forest. More than two decades later, sustained habitat restoration transformed about 1,000 acres of its core habitat, and surveys estimated the bird population at around 1,300 individuals. The Smithsonian notes that this recovery followed years of removing invasive plants, restoring native forests, and planting more than 500,000 native trees.A species confined to a shrinking forestThe Azores bullfinch, locally known as the Priolo and scientifically as Pyrrhula murina, is endemic to SÃ£o Miguel, the biggest island in the Azores archipelago, and its decline followed centuries of changes to the islandâs native vegetation. A 2011 study published in Bird Conservation International evaluated annual monitoring data from 1991 to 2008, confirming that the historical population decline had successfully halted and stabilised shortly after the 1999 conservation measures were enacted. Instead of a continuing downward spiral, this tracking window proved that protecting the remaining laurel forest on the eastern side of the island provided an immediate, vital lifeline against habitat degradation.The birdâs dependence on native vegetation made habitat restoration central to its survival. Jamie Ramosâ research, which was later published in Biological Conservation, helped establish the importance of the bullfinchâs diet and habitat preferences. The study showed that the species feeds on a range of native plants and their seeds, buds and other parts, meaning that replacing native forest with invasive vegetation could reduce both available habitat and food. Ramosâ work reportedly helped conservationists conclude that protecting and expanding native forest was more important than simply trying to manage the bird directly.Notably, the conservation situation was serious enough that the International Union for Conservation of Nature listed the Azores bullfinch as Critically Endangered in 2005. However, the formal protection of its core habitat had already begun by then, with the Pico da Vara/Ribeira do Guilherme area designated for bird conservation in 1999. This milestone established the legal framework necessary to secure international funding over the next four years.The process of removing invasive plants and rebuilding native forestFollowing the administrative steps, major restoration work began in 2003, when the Portuguese Society for the Study of Birds (SPEA), working with the Azores government and European Union LIFE funding, began a dedicated conservation programme. Smithsonian reported that the first five-year project concentrated on improving forest quality by planting native trees. Later LIFE projects expanded the work, including establishing a nursery capable of producing a large number of native plants.Conservationists had to remove the invasive vegetation that had displaced the native plants. Managed in sequence, the LIFE Priolo project ran from 2003 to 2008, followed immediately by the LIFE Sustainable Laurel Forest project from 2009 to 2013. These projects restored around 275 hectares of laurel forest, which is roughly 680 acres, while later projects continued the restoration in the protected area.This work restored around 1,000 acres of core laurel forest over approximately two decades, with more than 500,000 native trees planted. Specifically, the European Commissionâs LIFE program notes a broader project footprint of roughly 450 hectares (about 1,112 acres) actively managed. This restored core area ultimately acted as an ecological engine, improving environmental quality across the wider region.In 2010, the IUCN moved the species from Critically Endangered to Endangered when a comprehensive, modernised census estimated the population at 1,000 birds, and then to Vulnerable in 2016. These changes indicate that the Azores bullfinch had successfully moved away from its steep downward trajectory and achieved population stabilisation.By 2023, data published by the European Commission reported that the population had grown to around 1,300 individuals. Benefiting from the core restoration work, these birds successfully expanded out into nearly 5,000 acres of suitable regional habitat now available within the wider protected zone. While different wildlife survey methods can produce varying baseline numbers, such as a parallel annual report estimating 1,061 individuals, both data models confirm that the population has achieved long-term stability.Therefore, the recovery cannot be reduced to a single number or single intervention. Six LIFE projects have supported conservation work over decades, while invasive plants and introduced mammals remain threats. articles.body: Apple threw a farewell party for its outgoing chief at Apple Park on Sunday, spilling out of Caffè Macs, the cafeteria tucked into the ring-shaped Cupertino headquarters, and into the courtyard at its centre, where OneRepublic performed in the round. A photo on X shows Cook holding a guitar, standing with the band.About 200 people were there, almost all of them Apple employees, The Information reported. Somewhere in the evening, Cook did something he has done publicly only once before in his 15 years running the company. Speaking to the room, he acknowledged his partner and called him by his first name, Mike.Laurene Powell Jobs and Jeff Williams were among those who paid tributePowell Jobs, wife of Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, spoke at the event. So did Jeff Williams, the chief operating officer who retired last year, and Eddy Cue, who runs services and health. John Ternus, the hardware engineering boss taking over as Apple CEO next Tuesday, also offered remarks. There were no politicians and no celebrity parade, just a room made up almost entirely of colleagues.Tim Cook has kept his personal life off the record since coming out in 2014He came out in a Bloomberg Businessweek essay in October 2014, writing that being gay had given him "the skin of a rhinoceros", which he said came in handy in his job. He described the decision as a trade-off with his own privacy and said he did not consider himself an activist. In the twelve years since, he has spoken far more often about privacy as a principle than about himself.John Ternus becomes Apple CEO on September 1 as Cook moves to executive chairmanApple announced the handover in April. Ternus joined the product design team in 2001 and has spent almost his entire career at the company. Cook becomes executive chairman, a role Apple says will include engaging with policymakers around the world, and Arthur Levinson shifts from chairman to lead independent director.The Information also reports a smaller detail that tells you what Apple is going for here. articles.title: Man dies in crash after Stratford-upon-Avon police pursuit
articles.summary: Two women are also hurt and one remains in hospital in critical condition.
articles.body:
A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash after a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.

Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmingham Road shortly before 17:30 BST on Monday but the driver failed to pull over, Warwickshire Police said.

A pursuit began and 15 minutes later the Audi crashed into a white Ford Puma, the force added, with the Audi's 19-year-old male driver confirmed dead at the scene by paramedics.

The driver of the Ford, a woman, was seriously injured and remains in hospital in critical condition, while injuries to a second woman - her passenger - were serious but not believed to be life-threatening. An investigation by the police watchdog is under way.

Officers said after failing to stop, the Audi made off in the direction of the A46 before travelling back towards Stratford on the A439 Warwick Road where the crash occurred.

A number of other cars were damaged during the pursuit, police said.

Warwick Road was closed on Monday from the Marraway roundabout to its junction with Ingon Lane and Sand Barn Lane, with the stretch remaining shut on Tuesday morning.

A spokesperson for West Midlands Ambulance Service said paramedics found four patients in total at the scene.

They included a man who was in a critical condition to whom crews gave advanced life support.

"Despite their best efforts, it became clear that nothing more could be done to save him and he was confirmed deceased by ambulance staff at the scene," the spokesperson said.

A woman who was driving the second car suffered life-threatening injuries, the ambulance service confirmed, and was taken to hospital in a critical condition. She was said by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to be in her 70s.

A female passenger in the vehicle was also seriously hurt and taken to hospital, although her condition was not thought by the ambulance service to be life-threatening.

Injuries to another patient from the car were not believed to be serious.

Supt Steve Flavell said: "Our thoughts are with the families of everyone involved in this collision... at this extremely difficult time.

"We made a mandatory referral to the IOPC because a death had occurred following police contact.

"They have declared an independent investigation and we will co-operate fully with their investigation."

The IOPC said the investigation was at an early stage and confirmed its officials attended the police's post-incident operation to gather information.

"We understand the driver of a black Audi A3 failed to stop for police and was then pursued for around six minutes before the vehicle was involved in a collision with a car being driven by a member of the public," a spokesperson said.

"We are also appealing for any car footage of the pursuit that other motorists may have recorded. Our investigators can be contacted at 0300 303 5609 or by email: WarwickRoadPursuit@policeconduct.gov.uk

"We have met with the families of the driver and the seriously injured woman to explain our role and will keep them regularly updated throughout our investigation, which is at an early stage."

Manuela Perteghella, Liberal Democrat MP for Stratford-on-Avon, said the incdent was "incredibly tragic".

"My thoughts are with the families of all those impacted. We must now let the investigation take its course."

Works were carried out on Warwick Road two years ago, aimed at reducing the number of crashes in the area.

Warwickshire County Council added a one-way system, lowered the speed limit and implemented a protected turning lane at the Ingon Lane junction.

Street lighting was also boosted to improve visibility for crossing pedestrians at Fisherman's Car Park.

articles.title: In 2012, a 67-year-old Chinese duck farmer refused to leave his five-storey home; officials built a highway around it before paying him 260,000 yuan to move
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Explore the remarkable story of Luo Baogen, a 67-year-old duck farmer in China whose five-storey house resisted demolition as authorities built a highway around it, sparking international attention and discussions on property rights.
articles.body: In Wenling, an eastern Chinese city in Zhejiang Province, a five-story house once stood alone in the middle of a newly paved road, surrounded by a makeshift traffic circle. The house belonged to Luo Baogen, a 67-year-old duck farmer who had built it with his wife for more than 600,000 yuan around 2001. When local authorities cleared the neighborhood for a new access road, Luo and his wife resisted relocation for several years, even as workers built the road around their home.While 459 households accepted relocation, Luo did notIn 2008, the Wenling government planned to relocate about 459 households in Xiayangzhang to make way for a main road in front of the cityâs new railway station. The project required relocating 459 households in the village of Xiayangzhang, and by the time construction started, Luo and his wife were the only holdouts. The first offer was estimated at 220,000 yuan and then increased to 260,000 yuan. However, Luo contended that even the second offer was still far too low in comparison with what it would cost him to reconstruct another house, as he had already invested more than 600,000 yuan in building the previous one.Rather than wait for the dispute to end, workers paved a road around Luo's house, leaving the five-story building in the middle of a large roundabout. Photos of that scene started circulating online in late 2012 and made Luo's house one of the most recognizable Chinese "nail houses" (the term is used for buildings resisting demolition).Luo kept electricity, water and cable through the standoff Unlike many nail house holdouts, who are often cut off from basic utilities as pressure to leave mounts, Luo and his wife still had mains electricity, running water and cable television at the time of the report, based on the South China Morning Post. That made his case unusual among nail houses, where utilities are sometimes cut off to pressure occupants. As time went on, he continued to refuse the 260,000 yuan offer, saying it was far less than the 800,000 yuan he would need to build the same house elsewhere, while construction was completed and the road had not yet been opened to traffic.Luo accepted 260,000 yuan and a new plot of land Luo eventually signed a demolition agreement on November 30, 2012, after further talks with local officials and his family. Under the terms, the Wenling government paid him 260,000 yuan and provided a separate parcel of land for a new house, according to China's state Xinhua news agency, cited in a report from the Bangkok Post. âIt was never a final solution for us to live in a lone house in the middle of the road,â Luo Baogen told Xinhua. âAfter the governmentâs explanations, I finally decided to move.The excavators pulled down the house on the very next day, December 1, 2012, after pictures of the property garnered international media attention. According to Chen Xuecai, the head of Xiayangzhang village, Luo had grown tired of the attention, with reporters visiting the house daily during the final stage of the dispute. Luo's case became the most famous example of a dispute that has repeatedly occurred in China during large-scale development projects. Such disputes were common even in big cities like Chongqing, Shanghai and Guangzhou, where local governments or private companies sometimes built roads around a property whose owner refused to move.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Russian stadium says it won't host Kanye West gigs
articles.summary: Two planned concerts are thrown into doubt, but Russian promoters insist they will go ahead.
articles.body:
The Russian stadium that was scheduled to host two shows by Ye, the rapper also known as Kanye West, has said the events will no longer take place.

In a social media post , St Petersburg's Gazprom Arena said no rental agreement had been signed with the concert promoters. "Accordingly, the concert cannot take place on our site."

West would have been the first major Western performer to play Russia since it invaded Ukraine in 2022. The rapper is trying to rehabilitate his image after years of antisemitic remarks, for which he recently apologised.

Gazprom Arena acknowledged it had received complaints about West's planned appearance and stressed that it "was not and is not" responsible for his booking.

The stadium said in its statement that the sold-out concerts, scheduled for 10 and 11 October, had been organised by the Moscow-based Say Agency.

Posting on its Telegram channel, Say Agency said the stadium's announcement had come as a surprise.

"We learned about [it] at the same time as you did, through the media," the agency wrote. "As of now, the Ye concert has not been canceled," it added in a follow-up message.

"We are trying to contact the venue to find out the reason for the post and resolve the issue. We will keep you updated."

The BBC has contacted West's publicist for a comment on the uncertainty over his Russian shows.

In its statement, Say Agency said it announced the concerts earlier this month based "on an official letter that was approved by" Gazprom Arena.

The stadium subsequently sent a rental agreement, Say Agency claimed, and the agency acknowledged the contract had not yet been signed but said the deadline to do so did not expire until later this week.

Last week, Gazprom Arena had posted enthusiastically about the concerts on social media, calling Ye "the most influential musical artist of our time".

Fans reacted to its latest announcement with disappointment.

"This was the shortest concert of my life," responded one, under Say Agency's Telegram post. "It's a shame that the government is putting obstacles in your way," added another.

There is no indication that authorities intervened in the shows, but there has been opposition to West's booking from some Russian politicians.

Vitaly Milonov, a notorious conservative lawmaker, suggested the star should perform traditional Russian songs instead of his planned setlist, reflecting the anti-Western views of many nationalists.

"Maybe after this he'll stop his disgusting antics and become a normal person," Milonov added in a video statement.

West's antisemitic remarks began in 2022, when he made a series of offensive comments on social media that led to his accounts being suspended. Fashion brands like Adidas and Balenciaga also ended their relationships with the star.

The musician went on to declare he was "a Nazi", releasing a song called Heil Hitler and selling T-shirts featuring the swastika.

This January, West apologised in a full-page advertisement in the Wall Street Journal, writing: "I am not a Nazi or an antisemite."

Reflecting on a "four-month-long manic episode of psychotic, paranoid and impulsive behaviour", he said he was "deeply mortified" by his actions and that his bipolar disorder meant "you're manic [and] you don't think you're sick".

However, some questioned the timing of his statement - which coincided with the release of a new album, Bully, and the start of his world tour.

He held his first major concert in the United States in more than five years in Los Angeles in April, but planned shows in England, France, Italy and Poland have been cancelled over his past behaviour.

Say Agency acknowledged the controversy in a Telegram post last week , but defended its decision to bring West to Russia.

"Not everything Kanye West said should be forgotten," it said.

"Many people are talking about Kanye today. Many are trying to criticise him for words spoken during difficult times.

"But it's easy to judge based on a single statement. It's more difficult to listen to a person who has been changing the industry for decades. We listened, and we want to remind you."

articles.title: In 2017, Florida scientists tested mosquitoes around Burmese pythons; three mosquito species contained python DNA in their blood meals, suggesting insects could help locate hidden giant snakes
articles.summary: US News: Soon a mosquito may be assigned the job of hunting one of the Evergladesâ most elusive predators. For the uninitiated, Burmese pythons are one of the .
articles.body: Soon a mosquito may be assigned the job of hunting one of the Evergladesâ most elusive predators. For the uninitiated, Burmese pythons are one of the most concerning invasive species in South Florida, as they can hide in dense vegetation, wetlands, and remote areas, making them notoriously difficult to find. Now, researchers have examined a strange strategy: allowing mosquitoes to discover where the giant snakes may be lurking. In the journal PLOS ONE, a study by Lawrence E. Reeves called "Interactions between the invasive Burmese python, Python bivittatus Kuhl, and the local mosquito community in Florida, USA," appears to suggest something beyond imagination, where it is thought that mosquitoes might become python detectives. The idea was based on doctoral research by Lawrence Reeves, a post-doctoral researcher at the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Florida Medical Entomology Lab in Vero Beach. Reeves and his research team examined the interactions between Burmese pythons and mosquitoes, an ecological relationship that had been largely ignored. While the effects of pythons on the animals they eat are fairly obvious, we know much less about their interactions with animals that eat them or otherwise interact with them. The researchers collected mosquitoes from a Burmese python facility in Florida, where the snakes were housed in outdoor cages. And when they examined the blood within the mosquitoes, they found Burmese python DNA in the blood meals of three different species of mosquito. The discovery also opened up the unlikely possibility that mosquitoes could one day serve as biological trackers of hidden pythons. Scroll down for the details.How the technique would work"While a mosquito is feeding, it ingests blood from its host," the research paper reads. And if you can get the DNA from that blood meal, you might be able to tell what animal the insect was feeding on most recently. This means that mosquitoes caught in the wild could provide clues to the presence of Burmese pythons in an area. Rather than searching every marsh or clump of vegetation for a well-camouflaged snake, researchers could simply gather mosquitoes and test their blood meals for python DNA. This technique could be used to produce tiny biological surveillance devices from common insects.Why Burmese pythons are so hard to findBurmese pythons are a major detection challenge because they are extremely adept at avoiding humans, the study shows. Their coloration and semi-aquatic lifestyle provides them with camouflage and the ability to inhabit hard-to-reach wetlands and more remote habitats. They are large, and thus may seem easy to spot, but often the opposite is true. A python can hide itself in the vegetation or in places that are hard for people to reach.Researchers have tried various methods to locate the invasive snakes, including volunteers searching for pythons, specially trained detection dogs, and experienced snake hunters from Indiaâs Irula community. All methods have their limitations; manual searches can be time-consuming, and remote terrain makes access difficult. Mosquito-based detection could be another possible tool for identifying areas with pythons.From snake tracking to ecosystem surveysThe team believes the method can be used for more than just locating individual pythons. Testing mosquitoes for python DNA could help scientists track the invasive snakes and conduct biodiversity surveys. Mosquitoes can travel through areas that are hard for researchers to access directly, and they can potentially provide biological clues from places not easily reached by humans. The technique would not necessarily replace current methods of catching or removing pythons. Instead, it can help researchers narrow their search and identify places worth a closer look.Could mosquitoes spread diseases from pythons?This finding raises another important scientific question. Would mosquitoes that feed on Burmese pythons be able to pick up pathogens from the snakes and transmit them to other animals? Scientists have previously studied connections between mosquitoes, snakes and diseases. Other snakes are believed to be involved in transmission of viruses such as West Nile virus and Eastern equine encephalitis virus. Burmese pythons are also vulnerable to infection with some pathogens. Studies have found that snakes can become infected with the chikungunya virus and then infect mosquitoes, but the wider significance of this route is unknown. Thatâs why scientists want to know if mosquitoes feeding on Burmese pythons could help spread disease in the ecosystem of the Everglades.A little bug with a major potential roleThe finding illustrates how research on invasive species can go off in unexpected directions. A mosquito may be a tiny irritant compared to a giant python, but the blood it drinks can contain valuable genetic information about the animals itâs encountered. If researchers can make this approach work in the wild, mosquito surveillance could be another weapon in the fight to track Burmese pythons across South Florida. Right now the research is an interesting possibility: Instead of asking humans, dogs, or trained snake hunters to find the hidden pythons, scientists may be able to ask the mosquitoes where they have been.Images Courtesy: istockCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US removes Syria from terrorism list after 46 years - what it means for the Middle East country
articles.summary: US News: The United States on Monday removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, ending a designation that had been in place since 1979 and imp.
articles.body: The United States on Monday removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, ending a designation that had been in place since 1979 and imposing significant restrictions on trade, investment and financial transactions with the country.The move, which followed a 45-day congressional review, marks a further step in Washingtonâs efforts to deepen ties with Syriaâs new government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa. The US also revoked the designation of the Nusrah Front, later known as Hayâat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organisation. The Treasury Department announced corresponding sanctions relief.âThese actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism,â US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the measures would encourage investment and support Syriaâs economic recovery. âToday's action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability,â he said.The Treasury said the changes were âin line with President (Donald) Trump's promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syriaâ. It added that the removal of the restrictions âdoes not change Treasury's posture with regards to countering global terrorism and our commitment to hold bad actors in Syria accountable.âThe state sponsor designation had remained a major obstacle for businesses and financial institutions considering investment in Syria, even after the US ended its broader sanctions programme against the country in July 2025. The designation restricted US foreign assistance, defence exports and sales, certain dual-use goods and financial transactions.The Treasury has since said US financial institutions can provide services to Syria, process payments involving Syrian banks and establish correspondent banking relationships, provided sanctioned entities are not involved.Syriaâs government welcomed Mondayâs decision, describing it as an opportunity to reconnect with the global financial system and attract investment needed for reconstruction after nearly 14 years of war.Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani had earlier called the terrorism designation the âlast obstacleâ to rebuilding economic ties. âThere is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria,â he said.The US designation had been imposed in 1979, when Washington accused the government of then-President Hafez al-Assad of supporting militant groups. It continued under his son Bashar al-Assad, who was overthrown by rebels led by Sharaa in December 2024.HTS, formerly known as the Nusrah Front, was once affiliated with al Qaeda in Syria before breaking ties with the group in 2016. Sharaa later led the rebel coalition that toppled Assad and became president.With Syriaâs removal, Cuba, Iran and North Korea remain the three countries on the US state sponsors of terrorism list.The latest decision follows a broader rapprochement between Washington and Damascus. US President Donald Trump has backed sanctions relief for Syria and met Sharaa during a visit to Turkey, as the new Syrian government seeks international support for economic reconstruction.Syrian officials have also been pursuing closer links with international financial institutions and companies. The country's finance ministry has held discussions with Bank of America executives, while Mastercard has announced work with QNB Group and Syriaâs central bank to develop infrastructure for international card payments.Washington has said its engagement with Damascus is aimed at supporting Syriaâs stabilisation, economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy, while maintaining targeted measures against terrorism and other sanctioned actors.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: The 26-year-old faces up to seven years in jail for allegedly stealing a denim jacket from an airport shop in 2024.
articles.body:
Singapore has charged a British man for theft more than two years after he allegedly stole a denim jacket from a store at the airport shopping mall.

The police were alerted to the theft in the evening of 14 August 2024 when a retail assistant at Singapore's Changi Airport realised a blue denim jacket was missing from a display mannequin.

Surveillance footage showed a man removing the jacket, worth about S$350 ($275; £202), from the mannequin and leaving the store without making payment. By the time the authorities established his identity, the man had departed Singapore.

The 26-year-old was arrested on 15 August this year while in transit at the airport and was charged on Tuesday.

"The police take a serious stance of shop theft and will deal firmly with offenders in accordance with the law.

"Offenders should not assume that they can evade detection simply by leaving Singapore after committing an offence," the Singapore Police Force said in a statement on Monday.

In its statement the police also recounted a separate arrest of a 50-year-old Polish woman who had stolen two bottles of perfume from retail stores inside one of the airport's terminals on 11 June this year.

She was arrested in the transit area shortly before she was scheduled to depart Singapore. The woman was charged with two counts of theft on Tuesday.

Those convicted of theft in Singapore face up to seven years in jail.

articles.title: Deportees who refused to exit a U.S. flight in Liberia are sent to Equatorial Guinea
articles.summary: The six people from Cuba, Brazil and Cameroon were flown to another African nation as part of a third-country deportation deal with the Trump administration.
articles.body: DAKAR, Senegal — Six people who were deported by the United States to Liberia last week resisted getting off the plane and instead were sent to Equatorial Guinea, another African nation that signed a third-country deportation agreement with the Trump administration, a person on the plane and a lawyer in contact with the six said Monday. Under a series of often secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to two dozen countries that aren’t their own as it pushes ahead with its immigration crackdown, advocates say. Immigration lawyers say the practice is being used as a legal loophole to indirectly return some asylum seekers to countries they fled. The people who refused to get off the plane in Liberia on Thursday were four Cuban men, a Brazilian man and a Cameroonian woman, the person and the lawyer said. A Honduran deportee aboard the flight said the group refused to disembark, saying Liberia was “not their country” and that they would face danger there. They were then separated from the others, he said. He spoke on condition of anonymity out of fear of reprisals. He said the other passengers got off in Liberia because they feared officers would force them. Meredyth Yoon, litigation director for Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta, said the deportees who resisted leaving the plane in Liberia were told they would be returned to the United States but instead were flown to Malabo city in Equatorial Guinea. “It was a really heartbreaking and chaotic scene when they arrived in Malabo on Thursday,” Yoon said. Some arrived in chains and in extreme distress, she said, including the Cameroonian woman and one of the Cuban men, who Yoon said has a large abdominal growth and uses a colostomy bag that must be drained regularly. There is no medical staff at the hotel in Equatorial Guinea where the six are being held, alongside around 40 other deported migrants, she added. Conditions at the hotel have worsened in recent months, Yoon said, with food sometimes withheld and guards accused of threatening, beating and choking some of the migrants. Equatorial Guinea’s government did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Under an opaque $7.5 million deal with the Trump administration, Equatorial Guinea’s all-powerful president, Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, has turned the hotel owned by his family into a prison for asylum seekers deported from the U.S. One of the Cubans sent to Equatorial Guinea was Carlos Rodríguez López, 35, who had been living in Miami Gardens, Florida. Igrayne Ribot, his wife and the mother of their daughter, said in an interview with the Telemundo affiliate in Miami that news of her husband’s deportation “arrived all of a sudden.” After receiving a notification about her husband’s transfer, she was able to reach him via video call. He told her he was in Africa. “I broke down,” she said. “Nobody imagines something like that — it was terrifying.”

articles.title: In 2009, Iceland drillers hit 1,000°C magma by accident, unlocking a geothermal source that could produce nearly 10 times more power
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2009, a drilling operation in northeast Iceland unexpectedly punched into molten rock at Krafla, revealing one of the hottest geothermal resources .
articles.body: In 2009, a drilling operation in northeast Iceland unexpectedly punched into molten rock at Krafla, revealing one of the hottest geothermal resources ever reached by a borehole. The Iceland Deep Drilling Project(IDDP) had been searching for high-temperature geothermal energy, but instead of finding only hot water and rock, the drill encountered magma at about 2.1 kilometres below the surface. Temperatures there were estimated at roughly 900–1,000°C. What followed turned an accident into an extraordinary energy experiment. Engineers managed to complete the well and draw superheated steam from the area around the magma, showing that heat close to molten rock could deliver far more energy than geothermal wells. The result also gave scientists a unique glimpse into a part of Earth that is almost impossible to reach, setting the stage for a more ambitious attempt to study and use magma.1000°C magma encounter become an energy experimentInstead of simply abandoning the well, the project team decided to find out what the unexpected magma encounter could actually do. The engineers installed a steel casing in the well, with the lower section perforated near the magma. The hole was then allowed to heat gradually. Eventually, it began producing extremely hot, high-pressure steam. IDDP-1 produced superheated steam for roughly two years, until July 2012. During testing, the steam reached temperatures above 450°C, making the well the hottest geothermal production well in the world at the time. The steam could also be fed directly into the existing Krafla power plant. The result was much more significant than setting a temperature record. It demonstrated that a geothermal well could operate extremely close to molten rock and draw useful energy from the intense heat surrounding it.What was the drilling team looking for in IcelandThe team was searching for a better source of geothermal energy. The IDDP was established to investigate whether extremely hot underground conditions could provide much more energy than conventional geothermal systems. At Krafla, in northeast Iceland, the project planned to drill far deeper than the point where most geothermal wells normally operate. According to PhysOrg, IDDP-1 was intended to explore high-temperature resources, with the original drilling programme taking the well towards depths of around 4.5 kilometres. Instead, the drill encountered something completely unexpected at just 2.1 kilometres which was molten rock with temperatures of approximately 900–1,000°C. The discovery was extraordinary because drilling directly into magma is extremely rare. Therefore, Krafla became a natural laboratory where scientists could study what happens when a well reaches the boundary between solid rock and molten material.Why was the well so much more powerfulThe reason was the enormous amount of heat available at such extreme temperatures. Conventional geothermal wells generally rely on naturally heated underground water. Superhot geothermal systems aim to reach much hotter conditions, where water carries substantially more energy. The ‘Clean Air Task Force’ reported that IDDP-1 could have generated up to 36 megawatts of electricity, equivalent to roughly 5-10 times the output of a typical commercial geothermal well operating at lower temperatures. It also described the well as the world's hottest production well when it reached 450°C during operation. The reason is relatively simple that when ‘water is subjected to extreme underground heat, it can become superheated steam capable of carrying far more energy to the surface.’ That is why the accidental discovery became so important. The drill had not simply found hot rock; it had revealed a potentially much more energy-dense geothermal resource.Challenges created by the extreme heat inside the wellThe same conditions that made IDDP-1 powerful also made it incredibly difficult to operate. The ‘Clean Air Task Force’ noted that the project faced severe corrosion while the well was heating up. The casing also had to withstand exceptionally hostile temperatures and fluids. Once the fluid became sufficiently hot, however, corrosion decreased substantially. The experience showed engineers that future wells would need carefully designed casings, valves, cement and surface equipment capable of surviving these conditions.The project also faced mechanical setbacks. According to AAPG, the drill became stuck and the team had to sidetrack the well during the effort. The experience nevertheless produced valuable information about drilling through extremely hot and pressurised underground environments. Eventually, IDDP-1 was shut down in 2012 after problems with surface equipment. But the experiment had already proved its central point that extremely hot geothermal resources could potentially produce dramatically more electricity from a single well.Foundation of the Krafla Magma Testbed(KMT)The unexpected discovery did not end with the IDDP-1 experiment. Instead, it inspired a much larger scientific ambition. The Krafla Magma Testbed (KMT) was developed as an international project designed to create the world's first magma observatory. Its aim is to deliberately access magma at Krafla and study it directly rather than waiting for another accidental encounter. KMT says the site is particularly valuable because a known magma body exists at relatively shallow depth, making Krafla an exceptional place for controlled research.The ‘International Continental Scientific Drilling Program’ states that rhyolitic magma at Krafla is known to exist at roughly 2.1–2.5 kilometres depth and around 900°C. Researchers hope to examine the boundary between the magma and surrounding rock, while also keeping the well available for long-term observations. The planned work is about more than electricity. Scientists want to understand how heat and fluids move around magma, improve instruments that can survive extreme underground conditions and learn more about volcanic systems.Could magma become a new source of geothermal powerThe Krafla experience suggests that it could, although major engineering challenges remain. KMT describes superhot geothermal resources as having the potential to greatly increase energy output per well. The project is being developed as both a research facility and a testbed for technologies that could eventually make these resources easier and safer to utilise. The AGU report also noted that KMT could help researchers understand how heat moves from magma into the surrounding geothermal system. One earlier analysis suggested that long-term flows of superheated steam from the IDDP-1 area could potentially produce more than 30 megawatts of electricity from a single well. The accidental drilling of 2009 ultimately changed the direction of geothermal research. Today, the goal is no longer to avoid magma. Scientists and engineers are increasingly asking whether, with the right technology, they can safely reach it, understand it and perhaps one day turn its extraordinary heat into a dependable source of clean electricity.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
